knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Charts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth-manifold chart with Euclidean coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a topological manifold of dimension \(n\). A coordinate chart on \(M\) is a pair \((U,\varphi)\), where \(U\subseteq M\) is open and \(\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a homeomorphism onto an open set. The components \(x^i=\pi_i\circ\varphi\) are the local coordinate functions, and each \(p\in U\) is represented by \(\varphi(p)=(x^1(p),\ldots,x^n(p))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate chart identifies an open part of an n-dimensional manifold homeomorphically with an open subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((U,\varphi)\) supplies local Euclidean coordinates on \(M\).

notation.meaning: coordinate chart with domain U and coordinate map phi

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard, precise, and appropriate for the Coordinate Charts leaf, but no inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Compatible Atlases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth compatibility and maximal atlases on finite-dimensional manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An atlas on an \(n\)-dimensional topological manifold \(M\) is a family \(\mathcal A=\{(U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\}\) of charts satisfying \(M=\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha\). It is smoothly compatible if, whenever \(U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\neq\varnothing\), the transition maps \(\varphi_\beta\circ\varphi_\alpha^{-1}\) and \(\varphi_\alpha\circ\varphi_\beta^{-1}\) are smooth on their open Euclidean domains. A smooth structure is a maximal smoothly compatible atlas.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible atlas covers the manifold by charts whose overlap transformations are smooth; its maximal extension defines a smooth structure.
assumptions_latex: Each \((U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\) is a coordinate chart on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\) determines a smooth structure precisely through smooth transition maps.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atlas and smooth-compatibility definition fits the leaf and is mathematically standard, but it has no authoritative source reference or specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Atlas on a Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an atlas by mutual chart compatibility and coverage of the underlying set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An atlas $\mathcal A$ on a set $M$ is a compatible collection of charts on $M$ whose domains cover $M$. Equivalently, for every $x\in M$, there exists $(\mathcal U,\varphi)\in\mathcal A$ such that $x\in\mathcal U$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atlas is a compatible collection of charts whose domains cover the entire underlying set.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A\text{ is a compatible collection of charts on }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=\bigcup_{(\mathcal U,\varphi)\in\mathcal A}\mathcal U,\qquad \forall x\in M\;\exists(\mathcal U,\varphi)\in\mathcal A:\ x\in\mathcal U.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Atlases and Generated Maximal Atlas
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of smooth atlases of the same dimension on the same set and the maximal atlas they generate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A,\mathcal A_1,\mathcal A_2\) be \(d\)-dimensional smooth atlases on the same set \(\mathcal M\). The atlases \(\mathcal A_1\) and \(\mathcal A_2\) are equivalent if \(\mathcal A_1\cup\mathcal A_2\) is an atlas. Define \(\mathcal A^+\) to be the collection of all charts \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\) such that \(\mathcal A\cup\{(\mathcal U,\varphi)\}\) is an atlas. Then \(\mathcal A^+\) is the maximal atlas generated by \(\mathcal A\), and \(\mathcal A_1\) and \(\mathcal A_2\) are equivalent if and only if they generate the same maximal atlas. A maximal atlas on \(\mathcal M\) is a differentiable structure on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two smooth atlases of the same dimension on the same set are equivalent when their union is an atlas. All charts compatible with an atlas form its generated maximal atlas. Two atlases are equivalent exactly when they generate the same maximal atlas, also called a differentiable structure.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A,\mathcal A_1,\mathcal A_2\text{ are }d\text{-dimensional smooth atlases on the same set }\mathcal M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal A_1\sim\mathcal A_2\iff\mathcal A_1^+=\mathcal A_2^+,\qquad \mathcal A^+\text{ is a maximal atlas and hence a differentiable structure on }\mathcal M.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Coordinate Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate representation of differentials and tangent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:M\to N\) be smooth, let \(p\in M\), and choose charts \((U,\varphi)\) at \(p\) and \((V,\psi)\) at \(F(p)\). The differential is represented in coordinates by \(D(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))\). Thus a tangent vector with coordinate column \(v\) is mapped to the coordinate column \(D(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))v\). Under chart changes, these columns transform by the corresponding transition-map Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local charts turn manifold differentials into ordinary Jacobian multiplication, with transition Jacobians governing changes of coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([dF_p(v)]_\psi=D(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))[v]_\varphi\).

notation.meaning: coordinate column of a tangent vector in chart phi

knowledge_statements.statement_title: C-s Maps Between Manifolds in Local Coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines continuity as the C-zero case and positive-order regularity through source and target charts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be \(m\)- and \(n\)-dimensional \(C^r\) manifolds. A map \(f:M\to N\) is of class \(C^0\) if it is continuous. For \(s\in\mathbb Z\) with \(1\le s\le r\), a continuous map \(f\) is of class \(C^s\) at \(p\in M\) if there exist \(C^r\) charts \((U,\varphi)\) and \((V,\psi)\) containing \(p\) and \(f(p)\), respectively, such that \(f(U)\subseteq V\) and \(\psi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\to\mathbb R^n\) is of class \(C^s\) at \(\varphi(p)\). The map is of class \(C^s\) if this holds at every \(p\in M\). The composition \(\psi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1}\) is a local coordinate representation of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map between C-r manifolds is C-zero precisely when it is continuous. For positive orders through r, it is C-s at a point when suitable source and target charts give a C-s Euclidean coordinate representation there; it is globally C-s when this holds everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is }C^0\iff f\text{ is continuous};\quad f\text{ is }C^s\iff f\text{ is continuous and is }C^s\text{ in suitable local coordinates at every }p\in M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Action of a Vector Field on a Smooth Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines differentiation of a smooth function along the restriction of a vector field to an open subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a vector field on \(\mathcal M\), let \(\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal M\) be open, and let \(f\in\mathfrak F(\mathcal U)\). The action of \(V\) on \(f\) is the function \(Vf:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R\) defined by \[(Vf)(x)=\mathrm Df(x)[V(x)]\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathcal U.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector field V acts on a smooth function f defined on an open set U by taking, at each point x in U, the derivative of f in the tangent direction V(x).
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a vector field on \(\mathcal M\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Vf:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \((Vf)(x)=\mathrm Df(x)[V(x)]\) for all \(x\in\mathcal U\).

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent Bundle Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth tangent bundle of a finite-dimensional manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a smooth \(n\)-manifold \(M\), its tangent bundle is the disjoint union \(TM=\bigsqcup_{p\in M}T_pM\) with projection \(\pi:TM\to M\), \(\pi(v)=p\) for \(v\in T_pM\). For every chart \((U,\varphi)\), the map \(\Phi:\pi^{-1}(U)\to\varphi(U)\times\mathbb R^n\), \(\Phi(v)=(\varphi(p),d\varphi_p(v))\), is a bundle chart. These charts give \(TM\) a smooth \(2n\)-manifold structure and rank-\(n\) vector-bundle structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent bundle collects all tangent spaces and is locally a product of a manifold chart with an n-dimensional vector space.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a smooth manifold of dimension \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi:TM\to M\) is a smooth rank-\(n\) vector bundle and \(\dim(TM)=2n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tangent-bundle construction and bundle-chart description fit the leaf, but the smooth-manifold and vector-bundle assertions require an authoritative cited source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent Spaces, Tangent Bundle, and Vector Fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent vectors represented by curve velocities, the tangent-bundle construction, its possible global nontriviality, and vector fields as sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a $k$-dimensional differentiable manifold. For $x\in M$, $T_xM$ is the $k$-dimensional vector space of tangent vectors represented by velocities $\dot\gamma(0)$ of differentiable curves $\gamma$ in $M$ with $\gamma(0)=x$. The tangent bundle is $TM:=\bigsqcup_{x\in M}T_xM=\{(x,\xi):x\in M,\ \xi\in T_xM\}$ and is a manifold of dimension $2k$. In general, $TM$ need not be globally diffeomorphic to $M\times\mathbb R^k$. A vector field is a section $f:M\to TM$ satisfying $f(x)\in T_xM$ for every $x\in M$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each point of a k-dimensional differentiable manifold, tangent vectors are represented by velocities of curves through that point. The disjoint union of the tangent spaces is the 2k-dimensional tangent bundle, which need not be globally a product with R^k. A vector field assigns each point a vector in its tangent space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: TM=\bigsqcup_{x\in M}T_xM\text{ is a }2k\text{-dimensional manifold and need not be globally diffeomorphic to }M\times\mathbb R^k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent bundle and its natural atlas
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the tangent bundle, its foot projection, and the atlas induced by base-manifold charts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a smooth \(d\)-dimensional manifold \(\mathcal M\), define \[T\mathcal M:=\bigcup_{x\in\mathcal M}T_x\mathcal M,\qquad \pi:T\mathcal M\to\mathcal M,\quad \pi(\xi)=x\ \text{when }\xi\in T_x\mathcal M.\] If \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\) is a chart of \(\mathcal M\), then \[\xi\in T_x\mathcal M\longmapsto (\varphi_1(x),\ldots,\varphi_d(x),\xi\varphi_1,\ldots,\xi\varphi_d)^T\] defines a chart on \(T\mathcal M\) with domain \(\pi^{-1}(\mathcal U)\). The resulting collection of charts forms an atlas, giving \(T\mathcal M\) its natural manifold structure, called the tangent bundle of \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent bundle is the union of the tangent spaces, with projection sending each tangent vector to its foot. Charts of the base manifold induce base-and-tangent coordinate charts that give this union a natural manifold structure.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal M\text{ is a smooth manifold of dimension }d
(\mathcal U,\varphi)\text{ is a chart of }\mathcal M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\mathcal M=\bigcup_{x\in\mathcal M}T_x\mathcal M\text{ carries the natural atlas induced by charts of }\mathcal M

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent vectors as equivalence classes of curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic construction of tangent vectors on a smooth manifold using coordinate velocities of curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a smooth \(d\)-dimensional manifold, \(x\in\mathcal M\), and \(C_x\) the set of smooth curves \(c:I\to\mathcal M\) defined on an open interval \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) containing zero and satisfying \(c(0)=x\). For a chart \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\) about \(x\), define \(c_1\sim c_2\) if and only if \((\varphi\circ c_1)'(0)=(\varphi\circ c_2)'(0)\). This equivalence relation is independent of the chosen chart, and its equivalence classes are the tangent vectors to \(\mathcal M\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two smooth curves through x represent the same tangent vector when their coordinate representations have the same derivative at zero. This equivalence does not depend on the chart, and tangent vectors are its equivalence classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_1\sim c_2\iff(\varphi\circ c_1)'(0)=(\varphi\circ c_2)'(0),\quad [c]\text{ is a tangent vector at }x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quotient construction and linear structure of a tangent space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the tangent space from curve classes and its chart-induced vector-space operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a smooth \(d\)-manifold \(\mathcal M\) and \(x\in\mathcal M\), let \(C_x\) be the smooth curves through \(x\) and let \(\sim\) identify curves with equal coordinate velocity at zero. Then \(T_x\mathcal M=C_x/\!\sim=\{[c]:c\in C_x\}\). For every chart \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\) about \(x\), the map \(\theta_x^\varphi:T_x\mathcal M\to\mathbb R^d\), \(\theta_x^\varphi([c])=(\varphi\circ c)'(0)\), is well defined and bijective. The operations \(a[c_1]+b[c_2]=(\theta_x^\varphi)^{-1}(a\theta_x^\varphi([c_1])+b\theta_x^\varphi([c_2]))\) give \(T_x\mathcal M\) a linear-space structure independent of the chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent space at x is the quotient of smooth curves through x by equality of velocity. Coordinate velocity gives a well-defined bijection with R^d, and transporting the usual operations through this bijection produces a linear-space structure independent of the chosen chart.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_x\mathcal M=C_x/\!\sim,\qquad \theta_x^\varphi([c])=(\varphi\circ c)'(0)\text{ is bijective and induces a chart-independent linear structure}

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Vector Fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth sections of the tangent bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector field on a smooth manifold \(M\) is a section \(X:M\to TM\) of the tangent-bundle projection, so \(\pi\circ X=\operatorname{id}_M\) and \(X(p)\in T_pM\) for every \(p\in M\). It is smooth when \(X\) is smooth as a map into \(TM\). Equivalently, in every smooth chart with coordinates \((x^1,\ldots,x^n)\), there exist smooth functions \(X^i\) such that \(X=\sum_{i=1}^n X^i\,\partial/\partial x^i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth vector field assigns a tangent vector smoothly to every point, equivalently having smooth component functions in every chart.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\) is smooth exactly when its coordinate components \(X^1,\ldots,X^n\) are smooth in every chart.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth vector fields and their coordinate decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, action on functions, module operations, and local coordinate representation of smooth vector fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth vector field on \(\mathcal M\) is a smooth map \(\xi:\mathcal M\to T\mathcal M\) such that \(\xi_x\in T_x\mathcal M\) for every \(x\in\mathcal M\). It acts on \(f\in\mathfrak F(\mathcal M)\) by \((\xi f)(x)=\xi_x(f)\), and the pointwise operations are \((f\xi)_x=f(x)\xi_x\) and \((\xi+\zeta)_x=\xi_x+\zeta_x\). For a chart \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\), the coordinate vector fields satisfy \[(E_i f)(x)=\partial_i(f\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(x)),\] and every smooth vector field has the local decomposition \[\xi=\sum_i(\xi\varphi_i)E_i\quad\text{on }\mathcal U.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth vector field smoothly assigns a tangent vector to each point. Vector fields act as directional derivatives on functions, admit pointwise addition and multiplication by smooth functions, and decompose locally in the coordinate vector fields of any chart.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal U,\varphi)\text{ is a chart for the coordinate decomposition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi:\mathcal M\to T\mathcal M,\quad \xi_x\in T_x\mathcal M,\qquad \xi=\sum_i(\xi\varphi_i)E_i\text{ locally}

knowledge_statements.title: Local Trivializations of Tangent Bundles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chart-induced local product representation of the tangent bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a chart \((U,\varphi)\) on a smooth \(n\)-manifold \(M\), define \(\tau_U:\pi^{-1}(U)\to U\times\mathbb R^n\) by \(\tau_U(v)=(p,d\varphi_p(v))\) for \(v\in T_pM\). Then \(\tau_U\) is a diffeomorphism, is linear on every fiber, and satisfies \(\operatorname{pr}_1\circ\tau_U=\pi\). On an overlap, the fiber coordinate changes by \(w\mapsto D(\psi\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A manifold chart identifies the tangent bundle locally with a product, and overlap maps act on tangent coordinates through transition Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(TM|_U\cong U\times\mathbb R^n\) as smooth vector bundles.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate definition of smoothness between manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be smooth manifolds. A map \(F:M\to N\) is smooth if, for every \(p\in M\), there are smooth charts \((U,\varphi)\) about \(p\) and \((V,\psi)\) about \(F(p)\), with \(F(U)\subseteq V\), such that \(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\to\psi(V)\) is smooth as a map between open subsets of Euclidean spaces. Compatibility of atlases makes this definition chart-independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map between smooth manifolds is smooth when its expression in local coordinates is an ordinary smooth Euclidean map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is smooth exactly when its local coordinate representatives are smooth.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothness of maps between embedded submanifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines pointwise and global smoothness through local extensions to the ambient Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) and \(\mathcal M'\) be embedded submanifolds of \(\mathcal E\) and \(\mathcal E'\), respectively. A map \(F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M'\) is smooth at \(x\in\mathcal M\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) in \(\mathcal E\) and a smooth map \(\bar F:U\to\mathcal E'\) such that \(F(y)=\bar F(y)\) for all \(y\in\mathcal M\cap U\). The map \(\bar F\) is called a local smooth extension of \(F\) around \(x\). The map \(F\) is smooth if it is smooth at every \(x\in\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map between embedded submanifolds is smooth at a point when it locally agrees, on the source manifold, with a smooth map defined in the ambient space. It is smooth when this condition holds at every source point.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal E\) and \(\mathcal M'\subseteq\mathcal E'\) are embedded submanifolds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is smooth at }x\iff \exists\,U\subseteq\mathcal E\text{ open with }x\in U,\ \exists\,\bar F\in C^\infty(U,\mathcal E')\text{ such that }\bar F|_{\mathcal M\cap U}=F|_{\mathcal M\cap U};\quad F\text{ is smooth}\iff \forall x\in\mathcal M,\ F\text{ is smooth at }x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient-extension characterization of smooth maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes smooth maps on embedded submanifolds using one smooth extension defined on a neighborhood of the entire source manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) and \(\mathcal M'\) be embedded submanifolds of \(\mathcal E\) and \(\mathcal E'\), respectively. A map \(F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M'\) is smooth if and only if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\mathcal M\) in \(\mathcal E\) and a smooth map \(\bar F:U\to\mathcal E'\) such that \(F=\bar F|_{\mathcal M}\). In particular, \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is smooth if and only if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\mathcal M\) in \(\mathcal E\) and a smooth map \(\bar f:U\to\mathbb R\) such that \(f=\bar f|_{\mathcal M}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map between embedded submanifolds is smooth exactly when it is the restriction of a single smooth ambient-space map defined on a neighborhood of the whole source manifold. The same equivalence holds for real-valued functions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal E\) and \(\mathcal M'\subseteq\mathcal E'\) are embedded submanifolds.

knowledge_statements.title: Immersion Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immersions characterized by injective differentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M^m\) and \(N^n\) be smooth manifolds with \(m\leq n\). A smooth map \(F:M\to N\) is an immersion at \(p\in M\) if its differential \(dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N\) is injective, equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}(dF_p)=m\). It is an immersion if this holds at every point. Locally near each point, suitable coordinates put it in the form \((x^1,\ldots,x^m)\mapsto(x^1,\ldots,x^m,0,\ldots,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An immersion has injective differential everywhere and locally looks like the standard inclusion of a lower-dimensional Euclidean space.
assumptions_latex: \(M^m\) and \(N^n\) are smooth manifolds with \(m\leq n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is an immersion if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}(dF_p)=m\) for every \(p\in M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Submersion Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submersions characterized by surjective differentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M^m\) and \(N^n\) be smooth manifolds with \(m\geq n\). A smooth map \(F:M\to N\) is a submersion at \(p\in M\) if \(dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N\) is surjective, equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}(dF_p)=n\). It is a submersion if this holds everywhere. Locally near each point, suitable coordinates put it in the form \((x^1,\ldots,x^m)\mapsto(x^1,\ldots,x^n)\).

assumptions_latex: \(M^m\) and \(N^n\) are smooth manifolds with \(m\geq n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a submersion if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}(dF_p)=n\) for every \(p\in M\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local normal-form characterization of embedded submanifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes embedded submanifolds by local diffeomorphic flattening onto a coordinate subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal E\) be a linear space of dimension \(d\), let \(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal E\), and let \(n=d-k\). Then \(\mathcal M\) is an embedded submanifold of \(\mathcal E\) of dimension \(n\) if and only if, for every \(x\in\mathcal M\), there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\), an open set \(V\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and a diffeomorphism \(F:U\to V\) such that \(F(\mathcal M\cap U)=E\cap V\), where \(E=\{y\in\mathbb R^d:y_{n+1}=\cdots=y_d=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset is an embedded submanifold exactly when it can be locally transformed by a diffeomorphism into the standard coordinate subspace of the same dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M\text{ is an embedded submanifold of dimension }n\iff\forall x\in\mathcal M\ \exists U,V,F:\ F(\mathcal M\cap U)=E\cap V.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Embedded Submanifolds Admit Compatible Manifold Atlases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational compatibility of an embedded-submanifold structure with the topology inherited from its ambient linear space.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset that is an embedded submanifold in the stated sense has a manifold atlas whose topology is exactly its ambient subspace topology.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal E\) is an embedded submanifold in the stated sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M\) admits a manifold atlas and \(\tau_{\mathrm{atlas}}=\tau_{\mathrm{subspace}}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Embedding Space and Matrix Submanifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Introduces terminology for the ambient manifold of an embedded submanifold and for matrix-valued embedding spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose $\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal M$ admits a differentiable structure making it an embedded submanifold of $\mathcal M$. The ambient manifold $\mathcal M$ is called the embedding space. If $\mathcal M=\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ or $\mathcal M$ is an open subset of $\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, then $\mathcal N$ is called a matrix submanifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ambient manifold M is the embedding space of an embedded submanifold N. If M is a matrix space or an open subset of one, N is called a matrix submanifold.
assumptions_latex: $\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal M$ admits a differentiable structure making it an embedded submanifold of $\mathcal M$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal M\text{ is the embedding space; if }\mathcal M=\mathbb R^{n\times p}\text{ or }\mathcal M\subseteq\mathbb R^{n\times p}\text{ is open, then }\mathcal N\text{ is a matrix submanifold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Embedded submanifold and local defining function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines embedded submanifolds of a finite-dimensional linear ambient space, including open and positive-codimension cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal E\) be a \(d\)-dimensional linear space and let \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal E\). The set \(\mathcal M\) is a smooth embedded submanifold of dimension \(n\) if either: (i) \(n=d\) and \(\mathcal M\) is open in \(\mathcal E\); or (ii) \(n=d-k\) for some \(k\geq1\), and for every \(x\in\mathcal M\) there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) and a smooth map \(h:U\to\mathbb R^k\) such that \(\mathcal M\cap U=\{y\in U:h(y)=0\}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=k\). Such an \(h\) is a local defining function at \(x\). A linear subspace that is a manifold is also called a linear manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty subset is an embedded submanifold when it is open of full dimension or, locally at every point, is the zero set of a smooth map whose derivative has full rank. Such a map is a local defining function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M\text{ is an embedded submanifold of dimension }n\) under exactly the stated open-set or full-rank local zero-set conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Defining-Function Characterization of Embedded Submanifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes nonempty embedded submanifolds as open submanifolds or locally regular zero sets of fixed positive codimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \varnothing\neq\mathcal M\subseteq\overline{\mathcal M}, where \overline{\mathcal M} is a manifold. Then \mathcal M is an embedded submanifold of \overline{\mathcal M} if and only if either: (i) \mathcal M is open in \overline{\mathcal M}, in which case \dim\mathcal M=\dim\overline{\mathcal M}; or (ii) there is a fixed integer k\geq1 such that, for every x\in\mathcal M, there are a neighborhood \overline{\mathcal U} of x and a smooth map h:\overline{\mathcal U}\to\mathbb R^k with h^{-1}(0)=\mathcal M\cap\overline{\mathcal U} and \operatorname{rank}\mathrm Dh(x)=k. In case (ii), \dim\mathcal M=\dim\overline{\mathcal M}-k and \mathrm T_x\mathcal M=\ker\mathrm Dh(x)\subseteq\mathrm T_x\overline{\mathcal M}, using the identification induced by the inclusion map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty subset is an embedded submanifold exactly when it is open in the ambient manifold or, with a fixed positive codimension, is locally the zero set of a defining function whose differential has full rank at the point. In the latter case its tangent space is the kernel of that differential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal M\text{ is embedded}\iff\bigl[\mathcal M\text{ is open}\bigr]\lor\bigl[\exists k\geq1\ \forall x\in\mathcal M\ \exists(\overline{\mathcal U},h):h^{-1}(0)=\mathcal M\cap\overline{\mathcal U},\ \operatorname{rank}\mathrm Dh(x)=k\bigr];\quad\text{in the second case, }\mathrm T_x\mathcal M=\ker\mathrm Dh(x).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\varphi^{-1}(\mathbb R^m\times\{0\}^{n-m})=\{x\in\mathcal U:(\varphi(x))_{m+1}=\cdots=(\varphi(x))_n=0\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Level-Set Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular-value theorem for Euclidean equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be smooth, let \(c\in\mathbb R^m\), and suppose \(DF(x)\) has rank \(m\) for every \(x\in F^{-1}(c)\). Then \(M=F^{-1}(c)\) is either empty or an embedded smooth submanifold of \(\mathbb R^n\) of dimension \(n-m\). At every \(x\in M\), its tangent space is \(T_xM=\ker DF(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A level set with full-row-rank constraint Jacobian is an embedded manifold whose tangent space is the Jacobian kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(c\in\mathbb R^m\) is a regular value of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=F^{-1}(c)\) is an embedded \((n-m)\)-manifold and \(T_xM=\ker DF(x)\) for every \(x\in M\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Embedded Regular Level-Set Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular common-zero-set representation of a finite-dimensional embedded differentiable manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $h_i\in C^1(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R)$ for $i=1,\ldots,n-k$, and let $M=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h_i(x)=0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n-k\}$. If $\nabla h_1(x),\ldots,\nabla h_{n-k}(x)$ are linearly independent at every $x\in M$, then $M$ is a $k$-dimensional differentiable manifold embedded in $\mathbb R^n$. Equivalently, every point of $M$ is regular for this constraint representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The common zero set of n−k continuously differentiable functions on R^n is a k-dimensional embedded differentiable manifold if their gradients are linearly independent at every point of the zero set. Every point is then regular for the given constraint representation.
assumptions_latex: \{\nabla h_i(x)\}_{i=1}^{n-k}\text{ is linearly independent for every }x\in M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is a }k\text{-dimensional differentiable manifold embedded in }\mathbb R^n.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedded-submanifold structure and dimension of a fiber over a regular value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:\mathcal{M}_1\to\mathcal{M}_2 be smooth, where \dim\mathcal{M}_1=d_1, \dim\mathcal{M}_2=d_2, and d_1>d_2. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^{-1}(y)\text{ is a closed embedded submanifold of }\mathcal{M}_1,\quad \dim F^{-1}(y)=d_1-d_2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular Level-Set Submanifold Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives closedness, embeddedness, dimension, and tangent spaces for a nonempty level set whose defining map is surjective along the level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let h:\overline{\mathcal M}\to\mathcal N be smooth, let \alpha\in\mathcal N, and suppose \varnothing\neq\mathcal M=h^{-1}(\alpha). If \operatorname{rank}\mathrm Dh(x)=\dim\mathcal N for every x\in\mathcal M, then \mathcal M is closed in \overline{\mathcal M}, is an embedded submanifold of \overline{\mathcal M} with \dim\mathcal M=\dim\overline{\mathcal M}-\dim\mathcal N, and satisfies \mathrm T_x\mathcal M=\ker\mathrm Dh(x) for every x\in\mathcal M.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty level set on which the defining map has full rank is closed and is an embedded submanifold. Its codimension is the target manifold's dimension, and its tangent space is the kernel of the differential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal M\text{ is closed in }\overline{\mathcal M}\text{ and embedded},\quad \dim\mathcal M=\dim\overline{\mathcal M}-\dim\mathcal N,\quad \mathrm T_x\mathcal M=\ker\mathrm Dh(x)\quad\forall x\in\mathcal M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent space from a local defining function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the curve-defined tangent space of an embedded submanifold with the ambient space in the open case and with a defining-map derivative kernel otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be an embedded submanifold of \(\mathcal E\), let \(x\in\mathcal M\), and let \(T_x\mathcal M\) be defined through velocities of smooth curves. If \(\mathcal M\) is an open submanifold, then \(T_x\mathcal M=\mathcal E\). Otherwise, \(T_x\mathcal M=\ker Dh(x)\) for any local defining function \(h\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent space of an open submanifold is the whole ambient space. In positive codimension, it is the kernel of the derivative of any local defining function.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal E\text{ is an embedded submanifold}\)
\(T_x\mathcal M\text{ is defined by smooth-curve velocities}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M\text{ open}\Rightarrow T_x\mathcal M=\mathcal E;\qquad \mathcal M\text{ not open}\Rightarrow T_x\mathcal M=\ker Dh(x)\text{ for any local defining function }h.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent–Normal Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal splitting for embedded Riemannian submanifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be an embedded smooth submanifold with the metric induced by the Euclidean inner product. For every \(x\in M\), define the normal space by \(N_xM=(T_xM)^\perp\). Then the ambient space has the orthogonal direct-sum decomposition \(\mathbb R^n=T_xM\oplus N_xM\). Consequently every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) has unique components \(z_T\in T_xM\) and \(z_N\in N_xM\) satisfying \(z=z_T+z_N\) and \(\langle z_T,z_N\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each point of an embedded Euclidean manifold, every ambient vector splits uniquely into orthogonal tangent and normal components.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is an embedded smooth submanifold.
\(M\) has the metric induced by the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R^n=T_xM\oplus N_xM\) orthogonally for every \(x\in M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Projection Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal tangent and normal projectors for regular level sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=F^{-1}(c)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), where \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is smooth and \(J=DF(x)\) has full row rank at \(x\in M\). Since \(T_xM=\ker J\) and \(N_xM=\operatorname{range}(J^\top)\), the Euclidean orthogonal projectors are \[P_{N_xM}=J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}J,\qquad P_{T_xM}=I-J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}J.\] Thus any ambient vector \(z\) decomposes as \(z=P_{T_xM}z+P_{N_xM}z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For full-rank equality constraints, tangent and normal projections are explicit matrix expressions involving the constraint Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: \(M=F^{-1}(c)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a regular level-set manifold.
\(J=DF(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{T_xM}=I-J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}J\) and \(P_{N_xM}=J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}J\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean equality constraints with full-row-rank Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{M}=\{y\in U:c(y)=0\}\). The embedded constraint-qualification interface at \(x\in\mathcal{M}\) is the surjectivity condition \(Dc(x):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\). Under this condition, \(\mathcal{M}\) is locally an embedded submanifold of dimension \(n-m\), and its first-order feasible and normal directions are
\[
T_x\mathcal{M}=\ker Dc(x),\qquad N_x\mathcal{M}=\operatorname{range} Dc(x)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Thus ambient equality-constraint derivatives provide the tangent-normal interface used by manifold algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-row-rank constraint Jacobian makes the level set locally embedded; tangent directions lie in its kernel, while normal directions lie in its transpose range.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a manifold \(\mathcal M\), and let \(G=\operatorname{graph}(\sim)\). The conditions that \(G\) be an embedded submanifold of \(\mathcal M\times\mathcal M\) and that \(\pi_1:G\to\mathcal M\) be a submersion are necessary and sufficient for \(\mathcal M/\!\sim\) to admit an atlas making the canonical projection \(\pi\) a submersion. Such an atlas is unique, and its atlas topology equals the quotient topology. The condition that \(G\) be closed in \(\mathcal M\times\mathcal M\) is necessary and sufficient for the quotient topology to be Hausdorff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Embeddedness of the relation graph and submersivity of its first projection are exactly the conditions for a unique quotient atlas under which the canonical projection is a submersion; this atlas induces the quotient topology. Closedness of the graph is exactly the additional condition for that topology to be Hausdorff.
assumptions_latex: \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ embedded and }\pi_1\text{ a submersion}\iff\mathcal M/\!\sim\text{ admits the stated unique atlas}\); its atlas topology equals the quotient topology, and \(G\text{ closed}\iff\text{the quotient topology is Hausdorff}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and dimension of quotient fibers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes equivalence classes as embedded positive-dimensional fibers or discrete zero-dimensional fibers according to the quotient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M/\!\sim\) be a quotient manifold of a manifold \(\mathcal M\), and let \(\pi\) be the canonical projection. For every \(x\in\mathcal M\), if \(\dim(\mathcal M/\!\sim)<\dim(\mathcal M)\), then \(\pi^{-1}(\pi(x))\) is an embedded submanifold of \(\mathcal M\) of dimension \(\dim(\mathcal M)-\dim(\mathcal M/\!\sim)\). If \(\dim(\mathcal M/\!\sim)=\dim(\mathcal M)\), then \(\pi^{-1}(\pi(x))\) is a discrete set of points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the quotient has smaller dimension than the total space, each equivalence class is an embedded submanifold whose dimension is the dimension difference. When the dimensions agree, each equivalence class is discrete.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M/\!\sim\) is a quotient manifold of \(\mathcal M\).
\(\pi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M/\!\sim\) is the canonical projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\dim(\mathcal M/\!\sim)<\dim(\mathcal M)\), then \(\pi^{-1}(\pi(x))\) is embedded with dimension \(\dim(\mathcal M)-\dim(\mathcal M/\!\sim)\); if the dimensions are equal, then \(\pi^{-1}(\pi(x))\) is discrete.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quotient set, canonical projection, and quotient topology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational quotient-space structure induced by an equivalence relation on a manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a manifold \(\overline{\mathcal M}\). The quotient set is \(\mathcal M=\overline{\mathcal M}/\!\sim=\{[x]:x\in\overline{\mathcal M}\}\), and the canonical projection is \(\pi:\overline{\mathcal M}\to\mathcal M\), \(\pi(x)=[x]\). The quotient topology is defined by \(\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal M\text{ open}\iff\pi^{-1}(\mathcal U)\text{ open in }\overline{\mathcal M}\); with this topology, \(\pi\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quotient consists of the equivalence classes, and the canonical projection maps each point to its class. A subset of the quotient is open exactly when its inverse image is open in the original manifold; consequently, the projection is continuous.
assumptions_latex: \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation on \(\overline{\mathcal M}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M=\overline{\mathcal M}/\!\sim\), \(\pi(x)=[x]\), and \(\mathcal U\text{ is open in }\mathcal M\iff\pi^{-1}(\mathcal U)\text{ is open in }\overline{\mathcal M}\); hence \(\pi\) is continuous.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph characterization of regular equivalence relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives jointly necessary and sufficient embeddedness, submersion, and closedness conditions, together with the quotient-dimension formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a manifold \(\mathcal M\), and let \(G:=\operatorname{graph}(\sim)=\{(x,y)\in\mathcal M\times\mathcal M:x\sim y\}\). Then \(\sim\) is regular if and only if all three conditions hold: \(G\) is an embedded submanifold of \(\mathcal M\times\mathcal M\); the projection \(\pi_1:G\to\mathcal M\), \(\pi_1(x,y)=x\), is a submersion; and \(G\) is closed in \(\mathcal M\times\mathcal M\). Under these conditions, \(\dim(\mathcal M/\!\sim)=2\dim(\mathcal M)-\dim(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equivalence relation is regular exactly when its graph is an embedded submanifold, projection from the graph onto the first factor is a submersion, and the graph is closed. When these joint conditions hold, the quotient dimension is twice the dimension of the original manifold minus the graph dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sim\text{ is regular}\iff\bigl(G\text{ is embedded}\bigr)\land\bigl(\pi_1:G\to\mathcal M\text{ is a submersion}\bigr)\land\bigl(G\text{ is closed}\bigr)\), and then \(\dim(\mathcal M/\!\sim)=2\dim(\mathcal M)-\dim(G)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence classes, quotient sets, and quotient manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the quotient set and canonical projection, then defines a quotient-manifold structure by the submersion property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a manifold with an equivalence relation \(\sim\). Define \([x]:=\{y\in\mathcal M:y\sim x\}\), \(\mathcal M/\!\sim:=\{[x]:x\in\mathcal M\}\), and \(\pi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M/\!\sim\) by \(\pi(x)=[x]\). Then \(\pi(x)=\pi(y)\) if and only if \(x\sim y\), and \([x]=\pi^{-1}(\pi(x))\). A manifold structure on \(\mathcal M/\!\sim\) is a quotient-manifold structure precisely when \(\pi\) is a submersion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quotient is the set of equivalence classes, and the canonical projection maps each point to its class. Two points have the same image exactly when they are equivalent, and each class is a fiber of the projection. A manifold structure on the quotient is a quotient-manifold structure when the canonical projection is a submersion.
assumptions_latex: \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation on \(\mathcal M\).
A manifold structure is given on \(\mathcal M/\!\sim\) for the quotient-manifold definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([x]=\{y\in\mathcal M:y\sim x\}\), \(\mathcal M/\!\sim=\{[x]:x\in\mathcal M\}\), \(\pi(x)=\pi(y)\iff x\sim y\), \([x]=\pi^{-1}(\pi(x))\), and the given structure is a quotient-manifold structure iff \(\pi\) is a submersion.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: vertical space is the tangent space to an orbit and kernel of the quotient differential
No relevant differential-geometry source locator was supplied; authoritative source required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertical geometry of a regular group-action quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in M\), the vertical space is the tangent space to the fiber of the quotient projection:
\[
\mathcal{V}_x:=T_x\pi^{-1}([x])=T_x(G\cdot x)=\ker d\pi_x.
\]
Equivalently, if \(\mathfrak{g}\) is the Lie algebra of \(G\), then
\[
\mathcal{V}_x=\{\xi_M(x):\xi\in\mathfrak{g}\},
\]
where \(\xi_M(x)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\exp(t\xi)\cdot x\). Freeness makes the map \(\xi\mapsto\xi_M(x)\) injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The vertical space consists exactly of tangent directions along the group orbit, equivalently the kernel of the quotient projection differential.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertical Space Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vertical-space definition and its equivalent orbit, kernel, and infinitesimal-action descriptions are appropriate, but no source locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-orthogonal connection on a regular Riemannian quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At each \(x\in M\), define the horizontal space by
\[
\mathcal{H}_x:=\mathcal{V}_x^{\perp_g}=\{\eta\,\in T_xM:g_x(\eta,
u)=0\ \text{for every }\nu\in\mathcal{V}_x\}.
\]
Because \(d\pi_x\) is surjective with kernel \(\mathcal{V}_x\), its restriction \(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x}\) is a linear isomorphism from \(\mathcal{H}_x\) onto \(T_{[x]}(M/G)\). Metric invariance makes the family \(x\mapsto\mathcal{H}_x\) equivariant along each orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The horizontal space is the metric-orthogonal complement of the orbit directions and maps isomorphically onto the quotient tangent space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal splitting of total-space tangent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in M\), the vertical and horizontal spaces form the orthogonal direct sum
\[
T_xM=\mathcal{V}_x\oplus\mathcal{H}_x.
\]
Consequently, each \(\eta\in T_xM\) has unique components \(\eta^{\mathcal V}\in\mathcal{V}_x\) and \(\eta^{\mathcal H}\in\mathcal{H}_x\) satisfying \(\eta=\eta^{\mathcal V}+\eta^{\mathcal H}\). The associated linear projections obey \(P_x^{\mathcal V}+P_x^{\mathcal H}=I\), \((P_x^{\mathcal V})^2=P_x^{\mathcal V}\), \((P_x^{\mathcal H})^2=P_x^{\mathcal H}\), and \(P_x^{\mathcal V}P_x^{\mathcal H}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every total-space tangent vector splits uniquely into orthogonal vertical and horizontal components, with complementary idempotent projections.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertical–Horizontal Decomposition and Horizontal Lift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines total-space representations of quotient tangent vectors, vertical and horizontal spaces, and the unique horizontal lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal M=\overline{\mathcal M}/\!\sim be a quotient manifold with canonical projection \pi, let x\in\mathcal M, and choose \bar x\in\pi^{-1}(x). A vector \bar\xi\in T_{\bar x}\overline{\mathcal M} represents \xi\in T_x\mathcal M if \mathrm D\pi(\bar x)[\bar\xi]=\xi. The vertical space is \mathcal V_{\bar x}=T_{\bar x}(\pi^{-1}(x)). A horizontal distribution assigns a complementary subspace \mathcal H_{\bar x}\subseteq T_{\bar x}\overline{\mathcal M} such that T_{\bar x}\overline{\mathcal M}=\mathcal H_{\bar x}\oplus\mathcal V_{\bar x}. Once such a distribution is chosen, every \xi\in T_x\mathcal M has a unique \bar\xi_{\bar x}\in\mathcal H_{\bar x} satisfying \mathrm D\pi(\bar x)[\bar\xi_{\bar x}]=\xi; this is the horizontal lift of \xi at \bar x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient-manifold tangent vector may be represented by any total-space tangent vector mapped to it by the quotient projection. Vertical vectors are tangent to the fiber. Choosing horizontal spaces complementary to the vertical spaces selects exactly one horizontal representative, called the horizontal lift.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal M=\overline{\mathcal M}/\!\sim\text{ is a quotient manifold with canonical projection }\pi
T_{\bar x}\overline{\mathcal M}=\mathcal H_{\bar x}\oplus\mathcal V_{\bar x}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\xi\in T_x\mathcal M\;\exists!\,\bar\xi_{\bar x}\in\mathcal H_{\bar x}:\ \mathrm D\pi(\bar x)[\bar\xi_{\bar x}]=\xi.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient metric induced by an invariant total-space metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \([x]\in M/G\) and \(u,v\in T_{[x]}(M/G)\), let \(u_x^{\mathcal H},v_x^{\mathcal H}\in\mathcal{H}_x\) be their unique horizontal lifts. Define
\[
\bar g_{[x]}(u,v):=g_x(u_x^{\mathcal H},v_x^{\mathcal H}).
\]
Since the action is isometric, this value is independent of the representative \(x\) in its orbit. It therefore defines a Riemannian metric \(\bar g\) on \(M/G\), uniquely characterized by requiring \(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal H_x}\) to be an isometry for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Measure quotient tangent vectors by their horizontal lifts. Isometric group action makes the resulting inner product independent of the chosen representative.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent of differentiable objectives through a regular quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The objective \(f\) is group invariant when \(f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in M\). This holds exactly when there is a unique function \(\bar f:M/G\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(f=\bar f\circ\pi\). If \(f\) is differentiable, invariance implies
\[
df_x(\nu)=0\qquad\text{for every }\nu\in\mathcal{V}_x.
\]
Hence, for any metric defining \(\mathcal{H}_x=\mathcal{V}_x^{\perp}\), the Riemannian gradient \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\) is horizontal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective descends to the quotient exactly when it is constant on every orbit; its derivative then vanishes in all vertical directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric–Invariance Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility needed for representative-independent metric and gradient computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Metric–invariance compatibility requires every action map \(\Phi_a(x)=a\cdot x\) to be an isometry and the objective to be orbit invariant:
\[
g_{a\cdot x}(d\Phi_a\eta,d\Phi_a\zeta)=g_x(\eta,\zeta),\qquad f(a\cdot x)=f(x).
\]
These identities must hold for all \(a\in G\), \(x\in M\), and \(\eta,\zeta\in T_xM\). They imply \(d\Phi_a(\mathcal{H}_x)=\mathcal{H}_{a\cdot x}\) and \(\operatorname{grad}f(a\cdot x)=d\Phi_a\operatorname{grad}f(x)\), so quotient metric and gradient computations do not depend on the representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isometric group action and orbit-invariant objective make horizontal spaces and gradients transform equivariantly, ensuring representative-independent quotient computations.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts smoothly, freely, and properly on \(M\).
\(g_M\) is a Riemannian metric and \(f:M\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{a\cdot x}(d\Phi_a\eta,d\Phi_a\zeta)=g_x(\eta,\zeta)\) and \(f(a\cdot x)=f(x)\) ensure representative-independent quotient metric and gradient computations.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Lifting Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise lifting of quotient tangent vectors to representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in M\), the restriction \(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x}:\mathcal{H}_x\to T_{[x]}(M/G)\) is a linear isomorphism. The quotient lifting interface is therefore
\[
\operatorname{lift}_x:=\bigl(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x}\bigr)^{-1}.
\]
For every \(u\in T_{[x]}(M/G)\), its lift \(u_x^{\mathcal H}=\operatorname{lift}_x(u)\) is uniquely characterized by \(u_x^{\mathcal H}\in\mathcal{H}_x\) and \(d\pi_x(u_x^{\mathcal H})=u\). Under an invariant connection, lifts at different representatives are related by the differential of the group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient tangent vector has a unique horizontal lift at each representative, obtained by inverting the quotient differential restricted to the horizontal space.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:M\to M/G\) is a regular quotient projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lift}_x=(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x})^{-1}\) is the unique horizontal right inverse of \(d\pi_x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Grassmannian as a Stiefel quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of a p-dimensional subspace by the equivalence class of its orthonormal basis matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $1\le p\le n$, let $\operatorname{St}(n,p)=\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}:X^\top X=I_p\}$. For $X,Y\in\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, define $X\sim Y$ if $\operatorname{span}(X)=\operatorname{span}(Y)$. Then $X\sim Y$ if and only if $X=YQ$ for some $Q\in\mathrm O(p)$, and $[X]=\{XQ:Q\in\mathrm O(p)\}$. Hence $[X]\mapsto\operatorname{span}(X)$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{St}(n,p)/\mathrm O(p)$ to $\operatorname{Gr}(n,p)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For 1 ≤ p ≤ n, two orthonormal n-by-p basis matrices span the same p-dimensional subspace exactly when one is obtained from the other by right multiplication by a p-by-p orthogonal matrix. Thus the Grassmannian is in one-to-one correspondence with the quotient of the Stiefel manifold by this action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\sim Y\iff \exists Q\in\mathrm O(p):X=YQ,\qquad \operatorname{Gr}(n,p)\cong\operatorname{St}(n,p)/\mathrm O(p).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Preservation of minimizers and critical points under lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of optimization properties for an objective and its pullback through a manifold map, under property-specific hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi:\overline{\mathcal M}\to\mathcal M\), let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\), and define \(\bar f=f\circ\pi\). If \(\pi\) is surjective, then \(x\) is a global minimizer of \(\bar f\) if and only if \(\pi(x)\) is a global minimizer of \(f\). If \(\pi\) is continuous and open, then \(x\) is a local minimizer of \(\bar f\) if and only if \(\pi(x)\) is a local minimizer of \(f\). If \(\pi\) is smooth and \(\mathrm D\pi(x)\) is surjective at every point, then first-order criticality, and likewise second-order criticality, holds at \(x\) for \(\bar f\) if and only if it holds at \(\pi(x)\) for \(f\). All conclusions hold when \(\mathcal M\) is a quotient manifold of \(\overline{\mathcal M}\) and \(\pi\) is its canonical projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pullback through a manifold map preserves global minimizers under surjectivity, local minimizers under continuity and openness, and first- and second-order critical points under smoothness and an everywhere-surjective differential. Quotient-manifold projections satisfy all these conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:\overline{\mathcal M}\to\mathcal M\), \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\), and \(\bar f=f\circ\pi\).
For local minimizers, \(\pi\) is continuous and open.
For first- and second-order criticality, \(\pi\) is smooth, \(\mathrm D\pi(x)\) is surjective for all \(x\in\overline{\mathcal M}\), and the corresponding derivatives exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname*{argmin}\bar f\iff\pi(x)\in\operatorname*{argmin}f;\quad x\text{ is a local minimizer of }\bar f\iff\pi(x)\text{ is a local minimizer of }f;\quad x\text{ is first- or second-order critical for }\bar f\iff\pi(x)\text{ has the corresponding criticality for }f,\) under the respective hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection of total-space directions onto horizontal representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(\eta\in T_xM\), the horizontal projection is
\[
P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta:=\eta-P_x^{\mathcal V}\eta.
\]
Equivalently, \(P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta\) is the unique vector in \(\mathcal{H}_x\) such that \(\eta-P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta\in\mathcal{V}_x\). It satisfies \(d\pi_x(P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta)=d\pi_x(\eta)\), so removing a vertical component does not alter the represented quotient tangent vector. For an orthogonal splitting, \(P_x^{\mathcal H}\) is self-adjoint and idempotent with respect to the total-space metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizontal projection removes the vertical component of a tangent vector without changing the quotient tangent vector it represents.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal-Curve Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique maximal horizontal lifting of quotient curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A curve \(\gamma:J\to M\) horizontally represents \(\bar\gamma:I\to M/G\) when \(J\subseteq I\), \(\pi(\gamma(t))=\bar\gamma(t)\), and
\[
\dot\gamma(t)=\operatorname{lift}_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\dot{\bar\gamma}(t)\bigr)\in\mathcal{H}_{\gamma(t)}.
\]
Given \(t_0\in I\) and \(x_0\in\pi^{-1}(\bar\gamma(t_0))\), the associated first-order lifting equation has a unique maximal solution with \(\gamma(t_0)=x_0\). Conversely, every horizontal curve projects to a quotient curve whose velocity is \(d\pi_{\gamma(t)}\dot\gamma(t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient curve is represented by the unique maximal lift through a chosen representative whose velocity remains horizontal and projects to the quotient velocity.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:M\to M/G\) is a regular quotient equipped with a smooth horizontal distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique maximal curve \(\gamma\) through \(x_0\) satisfying \(\pi\circ\gamma=\bar\gamma\) and \(\dot\gamma(t)\in\mathcal{H}_{\gamma(t)}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local horizontal lifting and geodesic equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local existence and uniqueness of a horizontal lift through a prescribed representative, with equivalence of geodesicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:I\to\overline{\mathcal M}/\!\sim\) be a smooth curve on a Riemannian quotient manifold, where \(I\) is an open interval containing \(t_0\) and \(c'(t_0)\neq0\). For every \(x_0\in\overline{\mathcal M}\) satisfying \(c(t_0)=[x_0]\), there exist an open interval \(J\subseteq I\) containing \(t_0\) and a unique smooth horizontal curve \(\bar c:J\to\overline{\mathcal M}\) such that \(c|_J=\pi\circ\bar c\) and \(\bar c(t_0)=x_0\). On \(J\), \(c|_J\) is a geodesic if and only if \(\bar c\) is a geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonstationary quotient curve has a unique local horizontal lift through each chosen representative at the base time, and it is locally geodesic exactly when that horizontal lift is geodesic.
assumptions_latex: \(c:I\to\overline{\mathcal M}/\!\sim\) is smooth on a Riemannian quotient manifold.
\(I\) is an open interval containing \(t_0\) and \(c'(t_0)\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,J\subseteq I\ \exists!\,\bar c:J\to\overline{\mathcal M}:\ c|_J=\pi\circ\bar c,\ \bar c\text{ is horizontal},\ \bar c(t_0)=x_0,\quad c|_J\text{ is geodesic}\iff\bar c\text{ is geodesic}.

children.title: Nonfree Group Actions
children.top_down_role: Orbit structures with nontrivial stabilizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonfree Group Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete singular boundary caused by changing stabilizers and orbit dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the rotation action of \(G=SO(2)\) on \(M=\mathbb{R}^2\), the stabilizer is \(G_x=\{e\}\) when \(x\neq 0\), but \(G_0=SO(2)\). Thus the action is not free. Nonzero orbits are circles of dimension one, whereas the orbit of \(0\) has dimension zero. The orbit space is identified topologically with \([0,\infty)\) by \(q(x)=\lVert x\rVert\). The map \(q\) is smooth with rank one on \(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}\) but is not differentiable at \(0\). Consequently, the free-action quotient theorem and regular principal-bundle representation do not extend across the exceptional orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Planar rotations are free away from the origin but fix the origin. Orbit dimension changes there, and the radius quotient map ceases to be differentiable, so the regular principal-bundle quotient model fails across that orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The orbit space is identified with \([0,\infty)\) by \(q(x)=\lVert x\rVert\); \(q\) has rank one away from \(0\) and is not differentiable at \(0\), exposing singular behavior at the exceptional orbit.

notation.meaning: Special orthogonal group in two dimensions

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: planar rotation action is the canonical nonfree-action singularity example
No relevant transformation-group source locator was supplied; authoritative source required.

children.title: Singular Quotient Strata
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth or stratified regions arising in quotient spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Quotient Strata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit-type stratification of a proper, nonfree Lie-group quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly and properly on a manifold \(M\). For a closed subgroup \(H\leq G\), define the orbit-type subset \(M_{(H)}=\{x\in M:G_x\text{ is conjugate to }H\}\), where \(G_x\) is the stabilizer of \(x\). Each connected component of \(M_{(H)}/G\), when nonempty, is a smooth stratum of the quotient \(M/G\). The quotient is singular at orbit types for which the local orbit dimension or isotropy representation differs from that of the principal orbit type; the collection of strata forms the orbit-type stratification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper nonfree group quotient decomposes into smooth pieces indexed by conjugacy classes of stabilizers; nonprincipal pieces constitute its singular strata.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a Lie group acting smoothly and properly on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M/G\) is partitioned into orbit-type strata given by connected components of \(M_{(H)}/G\).

notation.meaning: Subset having stabilizer conjugate to H

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf and the core orbit-type stratification claim is plausible, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the proper-action hypotheses, smoothness of the strata, or the characterization of singular orbit types.

children.title: Regular-to-Singular Transition Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where smooth quotient-manifold descriptions cease to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular-to-Singular Transition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where the principal quotient-manifold model loses regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly and properly on \(M\), and let \(M_{\mathrm{pr}}\) be its open dense principal orbit-type subset. The regular quotient region is \(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G\). Its transition boundary in \(M/G\) is \(\partial(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G)=\overline{M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G}\setminus(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G)\). Approaching this boundary, the stabilizer type ceases to be principal; consequently the orbit dimension, quotient dimension, or local slice representation may change. A single fixed-dimensional quotient-manifold chart and its associated horizontal-space construction therefore need not extend smoothly across the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular region ends where stabilizer type changes; quotient dimension or local geometry may then change, invalidating one smooth quotient-manifold model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed-dimensional smooth quotient model is generally valid only on \(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G\), not across \(\partial(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the boundary identity and the claimed failure of fixed-dimensional quotient charts require a precise principal-orbit-type or slice-theorem source. The current source inventory supplies none.

knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian Product Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Riemannian geometry on a finite product of manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M_i,g_i)\), for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be Riemannian manifolds and set \(M=\prod_{i=1}^k M_i\). At \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), identify \(T_xM=\prod_{i=1}^kT_{x_i}M_i\) and define the product metric by \(g_x(\xi,\eta)=\sum_{i=1}^k(g_i)_{x_i}(\xi_i,\eta_i)\). Its Levi-Civita connection acts componentwise. Hence geodesics and exponential maps are componentwise, and the induced distance satisfies \(d_M(x,y)^2=\sum_{i=1}^k d_{M_i}(x_i,y_i)^2\) whenever the component distances are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite product carries the sum metric; tangent vectors, connections, geodesics, exponential maps, and squared distances decompose componentwise.
assumptions_latex: The product contains finitely many factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((M,g)\) has componentwise Riemannian geometry and \(d_M^2=\sum_i d_{M_i}^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits and the finite-product formulas are standard, including the componentwise connection and distance formula when all relevant points lie in connected components. No cited source with a relevant locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable Manifold Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential decomposition for objectives on product manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\prod_{i=1}^k M_i\) carry the product metric, and let \(f:M\to\mathbb{R}\) be smooth. Writing \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), the Riemannian gradient is the block vector \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=(\operatorname{grad}_1f(x),\ldots,\operatorname{grad}_kf(x))\), uniquely characterized by \((g_i)_{x_i}(\operatorname{grad}_if(x),\xi_i)=D_if(x)[\xi_i]\). If \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^k f_i(x_i)\), then each gradient block depends only on \(x_i\), and the Riemannian Hessian is block diagonal with diagonal blocks \(\operatorname{Hess}f_i(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a product manifold the gradient splits into blocks; for a sum of factorwise objectives, each block is independent and the Hessian is block diagonal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Factorwise separability of \(f\) implies independent gradient blocks and a block-diagonal Riemannian Hessian.

notation.meaning: Differential with respect to factor i
Riemannian gradient block on factor i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits, and the gradient and Hessian decomposition is mathematically plausible under the product metric and factorwise separability. It lacks an authoritative, specifically located source.

children.title: Redundant Factor Representations
children.top_down_role: Multiple factor tuples representing the same underlying object.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Factor Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonunique low-rank matrix factorization under invertible gauge transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(r\geq1\) and define \(\pi(U,V)=UV^{\mathsf T}\) for full-column-rank matrices \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\) and \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\). For every \(Q\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\), \(\pi(UQ,VQ^{-\mathsf T})=UV^{\mathsf T}\). Conversely, if \(U,V,\widetilde U,\widetilde V\) have full column rank and \(UV^{\mathsf T}=\widetilde U\widetilde V^{\mathsf T}\), then a unique \(Q\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\) satisfies \(\widetilde U=UQ\) and \(\widetilde V=VQ^{-\mathsf T}\). Thus a rank-\(r\) matrix is represented by an entire gauge orbit of factor pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-rank factor pair representing a rank-r matrix is nonunique: all equivalent pairs are related by an invertible change of latent basis.
assumptions_latex: \(U,V,\widetilde U,\widetilde V\) have \(r\) linearly independent columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(UV^{\mathsf T}=\widetilde U\widetilde V^{\mathsf T}\) exactly when \((\widetilde U,\widetilde V)=(UQ,VQ^{-\mathsf T})\) for a unique \(Q\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\).

notation.meaning: Group of invertible r-by-r real matrices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role exactly fits the leaf, and the stated GL(r) equivalence is standard for full-column-rank factors. No source or locator supports the converse and uniqueness claim.

children.title: Gauge Symmetry Orbits
children.top_down_role: Equivalence classes induced by transformations of redundant factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Symmetry Orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbits of a representation-preserving gauge-group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act smoothly on a parameter manifold \(P\), and let \(\pi:P\to X\) satisfy \(\pi(g\cdot p)=\pi(p)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(p\in P\). The gauge-symmetry orbit through \(p\) is \(G\cdot p=\{g\cdot p:g\in G\}\). Its tangent space is the vertical space \(\mathcal V_p=T_p(G\cdot p)\), which is contained in \(\ker D\pi(p)\). If every fiber of \(\pi\) is one orbit, then the represented objects are identified with the orbit space \(P/G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge transformations move parameters without changing the represented object; their orbit is an equivalence class, and its tangent directions are representation-null directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\cdot p\subseteq\pi^{-1}(\pi(p))\) and \(T_p(G\cdot p)\subseteq\ker D\pi(p)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, but X is not declared a smooth manifold and π is not assumed differentiable even though Dπ(p) and its kernel are used. A precise quotient-action source and corrected smoothness assumptions are required.

children.title: Gauge Identifiability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on recovering unique factors from an invariant representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Identifiability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between locally identifiable quotient parameters and additional degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) act on \(P\), let \(\pi:P\to X\) be invariant, and write \(\mathcal V_p=T_p(G\cdot p)\). Local identifiability modulo gauge at \(p\) requires \(\ker D\pi(p)=\mathcal V_p\) and locally constant orbit dimension. The gauge-identifiability boundary consists of points where either \(\ker D\pi(p)\supsetneq\mathcal V_p\) or the stabilizer dimension changes. At such points there are infinitesimal ambiguities not generated by the declared gauge action, or the quotient dimension changes, so a regular local quotient parametrization cannot be inferred from the gauge model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local identification modulo gauge fails when the representation has extra null directions or when stabilizer dimension changes, destroying a regular quotient parametrization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regular local identification modulo \(G\) fails when \(\ker D\pi(p)\neq\mathcal V_p\) or orbit dimension is not locally constant.

notation.meaning: Tangent space to the gauge orbit

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but kernel equality and locally constant orbit dimension alone do not establish a regular local quotient parametrization without additional constant-rank, fiber, and group-action regularity hypotheses. A precise source is required to determine the valid criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Stratification Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of fixed-rank manifold structure at lower-rank limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(0<r\leq\min(m,n)\), the set \(\mathcal M_r=\{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}X=r\}\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(r(m+n-r)\). Its closure is \(\overline{\mathcal M_r}=\{X:\operatorname{rank}X\leq r\}\), and its boundary is \(\bigcup_{s=0}^{r-1}\mathcal M_s\). Along a sequence in \(\mathcal M_r\) approaching rank \(s<r\), at least \(r-s\) positive singular values tend to zero. The fixed-rank tangent-space model therefore does not extend as a constant-dimensional manifold model through the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-rank matrices form a smooth manifold, but its boundary contains lower-rank strata where singular values vanish and the manifold dimension changes.
assumptions_latex: Matrices are real and finite dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\mathcal M_r=\bigcup_{s<r}\mathcal M_s\), and fixed-rank smooth geometry fails across this boundary.

notation.meaning: Set of matrices of rank exactly r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the displayed boundary formula is false for the ordinary topological boundary in the ambient matrix space: that boundary contains the rank-r stratum as well. The lower-rank union is the relative frontier of the rank-r stratum in its closure. No source is supplied to resolve and support the intended formulation.

children.title: Riemannian Distance
children.top_down_role: Global distance structure relevant to manifold optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Riemannian Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic length distance induced by a Riemannian metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a connected Riemannian manifold. For a piecewise continuously differentiable curve \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\), define its length by \(L_g(\gamma)=\int_0^1\sqrt{g_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))}\,dt\). The Riemannian distance between \(x,y\in M\) is \(d_g(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma}L_g(\gamma)\), where the infimum ranges over all such curves satisfying \(\gamma(0)=x\) and \(\gamma(1)=y\). This distance is finite and induces the original manifold topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Riemannian distance is the infimum of metric lengths of piecewise smooth curves joining two points, and it induces the manifold topology.
assumptions_latex: Admissible curves are piecewise continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_g(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma(0)=x,\,\gamma(1)=y}L_g(\gamma)\) defines the intrinsic metric on \(M\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits and the intrinsic-distance statement is standard for a connected Riemannian manifold, but no authoritative section, theorem, definition, or page locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Length of a piecewise-smooth Riemannian curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the curve-length functional used to construct Riemannian distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a Riemannian manifold and let \(c:[a,b]\to\mathcal M\) be piecewise smooth. Its length is \[L(c)=\int_a^b\lVert c'(t)\rVert_{c(t)}\,\mathrm dt.\] At partition times the derivative may be undefined; the integral is computed by summing the integrals over the finitely many smooth restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The length of a piecewise-smooth curve on a Riemannian manifold is the integral of its Riemannian speed, evaluated piece by piece across breakpoints.
assumptions_latex: \(c:[a,b]\to\mathcal M\) is a piecewise-smooth curve segment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(c)=\int_a^b\lVert c'(t)\rVert_{c(t)}\,\mathrm dt\), interpreted as the sum over the smooth pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint map of geodesics with prescribed initial velocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold and \(x\in M\). For every \(v\in T_xM\) whose maximal geodesic \(\gamma_v\) with \(\gamma_v(0)=x\) and \(\dot\gamma_v(0)=v\) is defined at time \(1\), define \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=\gamma_v(1)\). Its domain is an open star-shaped neighborhood of \(0_x\), and \(D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_xM}\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{Exp}_x\) is a diffeomorphism from some neighborhood of \(0_x\) onto a normal neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential map sends an initial tangent velocity to its geodesic endpoint at time one and is locally invertible near the zero vector.
assumptions_latex: The selected geodesic exists through time \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=\gamma_v(1)\) and \(D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_xM}\).

Then \operatorname{Exp}:\mathcal O\to\mathcal M is defined by \operatorname{Exp}(x,v)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=\gamma_v(1), with \mathcal O_x=\{v\in T_x\mathcal M:(x,v)\in\mathcal O\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential map, geodesic completeness, and normal neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects the local geodesic existence and scaling properties used to define the affine-connection exponential map, together with completeness and local normal-neighborhood properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mathcal M$ be a manifold endowed with an affine connection. For every $x\in\mathcal M$ and $\xi\in T_x\mathcal M$, there is an interval about $0$ and a unique geodesic $\gamma(t;x,\xi)$ satisfying $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\dot\gamma(0)=\xi$, and $\gamma(t;x,a\xi)=\gamma(at;x,\xi)$ whenever both sides are defined. Wherever the time-one geodesic exists, define $\operatorname{Exp}_x(\xi)=\gamma(1;x,\xi)$. The manifold is geodesically complete when $\operatorname{Exp}_x$ is defined on all of $T_x\mathcal M$ for every $x$. Locally, $\operatorname{Exp}_x$ is a diffeomorphism from a neighborhood of $0_x$ onto a neighborhood of $x$; if the tangent-space neighborhood is star-shaped, its image is a normal neighborhood of $x$. Moreover, $\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=x$ and $D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)[\xi]=\xi$ under the canonical identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initial position and velocity determine a unique local geodesic, with a scaling law where both geodesics are defined. Its time-one endpoint defines the exponential map on its natural domain. The map fixes the zero vector, has identity differential there, and is locally invertible. Full tangent-space domains characterize geodesic completeness, while star-shaped local inverse domains yield normal neighborhoods.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal M\text{ is a manifold endowed with an affine connection}
\text{The scaling identity and time-one evaluation are asserted only where the relevant geodesics are defined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Exp}_x(\xi)=\gamma(1;x,\xi),\quad \operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=x,\quad D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M},\quad \operatorname{Exp}_x\text{ is a local diffeomorphism at }0_x;\ \mathcal M\text{ is geodesically complete iff every }\operatorname{Exp}_x\text{ has domain }T_x\mathcal M.
