knowledge_statements.title: Model-Accuracy Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure when a trust-region model lacks first-order consistency with the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), at \(x=0\), let \(f(y)=y\), \(m(s)=-s\), and \(\Delta>0\). The minimizer of \(m\) over \(|s|\leq\Delta\) is \(s=\Delta\). Its predicted decrease is \(\Delta\), its actual decrease is \(-\Delta\), and its acceptance ratio is \(\rho=-1\). Therefore any trust-region rule requiring \(\rho\geq\eta\) for some \(\eta>0\) rejects the trial. Here \(m'(0)=-1\neq f'(0)=1\), so first-order model consistency fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model with the opposite gradient predicts decrease exactly where the objective increases, producing acceptance ratio minus one and rejection under any positive acceptance threshold.
assumptions_latex: The manifold is \(\mathbb R\), the current point is \(x=0\), and the trust-region radius is \(\Delta>0\).
The objective and model are \(f(y)=y\) and \(m(s)=-s\).
A trial is accepted only if its reduction ratio satisfies \(\rho\geq\eta\) for a prescribed \(\eta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model-minimizing step is \(s=\Delta\), its acceptance ratio is \(\rho=-1\), and it is rejected.

notation.meaning: Ratio of actual to predicted decrease

children.title: Correction-Subspace Geometry

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold and \(\mathcal E\) is a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C_x=\operatorname{range}(J_x^*)=(\ker J_x)^\perp\), and \(-J_x^\dagger F(x)\in\mathcal C_x\) is the minimum-norm minimizer of \(\lVert J_x\eta+F(x)\rVert\).

notation.meaning: Differential of the residual map at x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional adjoint range-kernel decomposition and Moore-Penrose least-squares geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-space correction geometry for a differentiable residual equation on a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal E\) be differentiable, where \(\mathcal M\) is a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold and \(\mathcal E\) is a finite-dimensional inner-product space. At \(x\in\mathcal M\), let \(J_x=\mathrm DF(x):T_x\mathcal M\to\mathcal E\). Define the active correction subspace by
\[\mathcal C_x=\operatorname{range}(J_x^*)=(\ker J_x)^\perp.\]
Then
\[T_x\mathcal M=\mathcal C_x\oplus\ker J_x.\]
The vector \(\eta_x=-J_x^\dagger F(x)\in\mathcal C_x\) is the minimum-norm minimizer of \(\lVert J_x\eta+F(x)\rVert\) over \(\eta\in T_x\mathcal M\). It solves \(J_x\eta=-F(x)\) exactly only when \(F(x)\in\operatorname{range}(J_x)\). Directions in \(\ker J_x\) are first-order residual-neutral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The active correction space is the orthogonal complement of the residual differential's kernel. The pseudoinverse gives the minimum-norm linearized least-squares correction in that space, and it is an exact residual correction only when the residual lies in the differential's range.
knowledge_statements.title: Correction-Subspace Geometry

children.top_down_role: Poor extraction, spectral clustering, or ineffective expansion causing stalled progress.

\(S_x\) is a linear subspace of \(T_x\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(F(x)\ne0\), first-order subspace stagnation is equivalent to \(P_{S_x}J_x^*F(x)=0\), in which case \(\mathrm D\phi(x)[\eta]=0\) for every \(\eta\in S_x\).

notation.meaning: Differential of the residual map at x
Orthogonal projector onto the correction subspace

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary at which a correction subspace contains no direction of strict first-order decrease for the squared residual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal E\) be differentiable, let \(J_x=\mathrm DF(x)\), let \(S_x\subseteq T_x\mathcal M\) be a linear correction subspace, and define \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert^2\). For \(F(x)\ne0\), first-order subspace stagnation occurs exactly when
\[P_{S_x}\operatorname{grad}\phi(x)=P_{S_x}J_x^*F(x)=0.\]
At this boundary, \(\mathrm D\phi(x)[\eta]=0\) for every \(\eta\in S_x\), so no direction in \(S_x\) gives strict first-order decrease of \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero residual is at the first-order subspace-stagnation boundary when its squared-norm gradient is orthogonal to the correction subspace. Every direction in that subspace then has zero directional derivative for the squared residual norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Subspace Stagnation Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Rank Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies a residual equation locally by the rank behavior of its differential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a smooth residual map \(F:\mathcal M^n\to\mathcal E^m\) and a point \(x_\star\), define three local rank regimes for \(J_x=\mathrm DF(x)\): (i) the full-rank regime, where \(\operatorname{rank}J_x=\min\{n,m\}\) throughout a neighborhood of \(x_\star\); (ii) the constant-deficient-rank regime, where \(\operatorname{rank}J_x=r<\min\{n,m\}\) throughout such a neighborhood; and (iii) the rank-varying regime, where every neighborhood of \(x_\star\) contains points at which \(J_x\) has different ranks. These regimes distinguish uniformly regular residual geometry from persistent degeneracy and rank loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual geometry is full rank, constantly rank deficient, or rank varying near a reference point, according to the local rank of the residual differential.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathcal M^n\to\mathcal E^m\) is continuously differentiable near \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of the stated full-rank, constant-deficient-rank, or rank-varying local regimes applies at \(x_\star\).

children.title: Local-Convergence Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Convergence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error-recursion classification of local convergence for retracted Riemannian iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\eta_k)\) converge to \(x_\star\), and let \(e_k=d(x_k,x_\star)\). The iteration is locally linear if there exist \(q\in(0,1)\) and \(k_0\) such that \(e_{k+1}\le q e_k\) for \(k\ge k_0\); superlinear if \(e_{k+1}/e_k\to0\); and of order \(p>1\) if \(0<\limsup_{k\to\infty}e_{k+1}/e_k^p<\infty\). Quadratic convergence is the case \(p=2\). These definitions are intrinsic because they use Riemannian distance rather than coordinate errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local convergence is linear, superlinear, or order p according to the asymptotic recursion for Riemannian distance to the limit; quadratic convergence has order two.
assumptions_latex: \(x_k\to x_\star\) and \(x_k\ne x_\star\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).
The iterates lie in a normal neighborhood of \(x_\star\) eventually.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic behavior of \(e_{k+1}\) relative to \(e_k\) determines the stated local-convergence regime.

notation.meaning: Riemannian distance from the kth iterate to the limit

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard intrinsic definitions of local convergence order

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linear and superlinear clauses are standard, but the displayed limsup condition may denote Q-order, order at least p, or exact order depending on convention. A source with a specific definition or page is needed before fixing this taxonomy-level regime statement.

children.title: Rank–Rate Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Influence of residual structure plus differential rank on attainable local rates.

assumptions_latex: \(F(x_\star)=0\), and \(J_x:T_x\mathcal M\to\mathcal E\) is an isomorphism with uniformly bounded inverse near \(x_\star\).
After vector transport to a common tangent space, \(J\) is locally Hölder continuous with exponent \(\alpha\in(0,1]\).
\(R\) is a second-order retraction, and each Newton equation is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all sufficiently close initial points, \(d(x_{k+1},x_\star)\le C d(x_k,x_\star)^{1+\alpha}\); in particular, \(\alpha=1\) yields quadratic convergence.

notation.meaning: Holder exponent of the transported differential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local rate transfer for an exactly solved Riemannian Newton iteration with an invertible Hölder-continuous residual differential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal E\) satisfy \(F(x_\star)=0\). Suppose that, throughout a neighborhood of \(x_\star\), \(J_x=\mathrm DF(x):T_x\mathcal M\to\mathcal E\) is an isomorphism and \(\lVert J_x^{-1}\rVert\le\beta\) for some \(\beta>0\). Assume, after vector transport to a common tangent space, that \(J\) is Hölder continuous with exponent \(\alpha\in(0,1]\). Let \(\eta_k\) be the unique solution of \(J_{x_k}\eta_k=-F(x_k)\), and set \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\eta_k)\) using a second-order retraction \(R\). Under the remaining local regularity hypotheses of the applicable Riemannian Newton theorem, there is a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every sufficiently close initial point,
\[d(x_{k+1},x_\star)\le C d(x_k,x_\star)^{1+\alpha}.\]
Consequently, \(\alpha=1\) gives quadratic local convergence. Loss of the uniform inverse bound removes this rate conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the residual differential is locally invertible with uniformly bounded inverse and is Holder continuous with exponent alpha, an exactly solved retracted Newton iteration has local order 1+alpha under the applicable manifold regularity assumptions. A Lipschitz differential gives quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank–Rate Correspondence

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Loss Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth residual equation showing loss of isolation and Newton-rate guarantees when rank drops.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2\) defined by \(F(x,y)=(x,xy)\). Its Jacobian is
\[J(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\y&x\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det J(x,y)=x.\]
For \(x\ne0\), the exact Newton step is \((\Delta x,\Delta y)=(-x,0)\), so one step reaches \((0,y)\). At every such point the Jacobian has rank one and \(F(0,y)=0\); hence the zero is not isolated and the iteration need not converge to the selected solution \((0,0)\). Rank loss therefore destroys the local inverse bound underlying a pointwise superlinear or quadratic convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For F(x,y)=(x,xy), Newton reaches the nonisolated solution line x=0, where the Jacobian loses rank. Convergence to the selected root cannot be guaranteed.
assumptions_latex: Newton steps are defined by \(J(x,y)(\Delta x,\Delta y)=-F(x,y)\) whenever \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank loss at \(x=0\) eliminates root isolation and any uniform Newton-rate guarantee toward \((0,0)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Cubic Regularization on Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Riemannian cubic-regularization iteration based on a retracted second-order model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathcal M\), regularization parameters \(\sigma_k>0\), and a retraction \(R\), define on \(T_{x_k}\mathcal M\)
\[m_k(\eta)=f(x_k)+\langle g_k,\eta\rangle+\tfrac12\langle\eta,H_k\eta\rangle+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\lVert\eta\rVert^3,\]
where \(g_k=\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\) and \(H_k=\operatorname{Hess}f(x_k)\). Choose a global minimizer \(\eta_k\) of \(m_k\), set \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\eta_k)\), and stop when \(\lVert g_k\rVert\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(H_k)\ge-\varepsilon_H\). The output is the first iterate satisfying both tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iterate, minimize a Hessian model plus a cubic step penalty in the tangent space, retract the step, and stop at approximate second-order stationarity.
assumptions_latex: Each tangent-space cubic model has a global minimizer.
\(R\) is a retraction defined at the computed steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method returns an \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\)-approximate second-order stationary point when its stopping test succeeds.

notation.meaning: Riemannian gradient at the kth iterate
Riemannian Hessian at the kth iterate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical cubic-regularization model transferred to a tangent space

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Regularization Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance-ratio framework for adaptive regularization of Riemannian tangent-space models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \(x_k\), approximately minimize a regularized model \(m_k\) on \(T_{x_k}\mathcal M\) to obtain \(\eta_k\), and compute
\[\rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(R_{x_k}(\eta_k))}{m_k(0)-m_k(\eta_k)}.\]
For thresholds \(0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1\), accept \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\eta_k)\) when \(\rho_k\ge\eta_1\), and otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=x_k\). Increase the regularization parameter when \(\rho_k<\eta_1\), decrease it when \(\rho_k\ge\eta_2\), and leave it within prescribed positive bounds otherwise. Stop when the selected first- or second-order stationarity test holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive regularization accepts steps by comparing actual and predicted decrease, strengthening regularization after poor agreement and weakening it after very good agreement.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is defined at every trial step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ratio \(\rho_k\) determines both step acceptance and the next regularization strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Second-Order Complexity Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case evaluation complexity of Riemannian cubic regularization under uniform pullback regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f\) is bounded below and the retraction pullbacks have uniformly Lipschitz Hessians on all trial-step neighborhoods. An adaptive Riemannian cubic-regularization method whose subproblems provide standard model decrease requires at most
\[O\!\left(\max\{\varepsilon_g^{-3/2},\varepsilon_H^{-3}\}\right)\]
successful iterations, and the same order of gradient/Hessian evaluations up to bounded unsuccessful trials, to produce \(x\) satisfying \(\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x)\rVert\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\ge-\varepsilon_H\). For first-order stationarity alone, the bound reduces to \(O(\varepsilon_g^{-3/2})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With Lipschitz pullback Hessians and sufficient model decrease, cubic regularization reaches approximate second-order stationarity in order max(epsilon-gradient^-3/2, epsilon-Hessian^-3) evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below on the relevant level set.
Retraction pullbacks have a uniform Lipschitz-Hessian constant.
Each subproblem step satisfies the required cubic-model decrease conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The evaluation bound is \(O(\max\{\varepsilon_g^{-3/2},\varepsilon_H^{-3}\})\), or \(O(\varepsilon_g^{-3/2})\) for first-order stationarity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponents are plausible for cubic regularization, but the stated successful-iteration and gradient/Hessian-evaluation bounds depend on precise pullback regularity, subproblem conditions, parameter-update rules, and a bound relating unsuccessful to successful trials. Those hypotheses are currently placeholders, so an exact theorem source is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Regularized-Subproblem Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable first- and second-order conditions for an inexact cubic-model step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the cubic model
\[m_k(\eta)=f(x_k)+\langle g_k,\eta\rangle+\tfrac12\langle\eta,H_k\eta\rangle+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\lVert\eta\rVert^3,\]
an inexact step \(\eta_k\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M\) is admissible when it gives positive predicted decrease and satisfies
\[m_k(0)-m_k(\eta_k)\ge\kappa_d\sigma_k\lVert\eta_k\rVert^3,\quad
\lVert\nabla m_k(\eta_k)\rVert\le\kappa_g\lVert\eta_k\rVert^2,\quad
\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2m_k(\eta_k))\ge-\kappa_H\lVert\eta_k\rVert,\]
for fixed constants \(\kappa_d>0\) and \(\kappa_g,\kappa_H\ge0\). A first-order interface may omit the final curvature condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact cubic step must achieve cubic-scale model decrease and small model gradient; second-order guarantees additionally require controlled negative curvature of the model.
assumptions_latex: Model derivatives use the tangent-space inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed decrease, gradient-residual, and curvature inequalities define an admissible inexact subproblem solution.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inequalities define a mathematically coherent condition, but it is unclear which established inexact cubic-subproblem interface they represent or whether this exact combination and scaling supports the intended first- and second-order complexity results. A specific theorem or algorithm locator is needed.

children.title: Riemannian Sampled-Objective Optimization
children.top_down_role: Online, minibatch, variance-reduced, adaptive, and finite-sum methods with their geometric comparison mechanisms and complexity families.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Hosseini and Sra, Recent Advances in Stochastic Riemannian Optimization
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Stochastic gradient through variance-reduced methods and convergence summary
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Hosseini and Sra, Recent Advances in Stochastic Riemannian Optimization

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Retraction, vector transport, variants, and convergence
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Sato, Kasai, and Mishra, Riemannian Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient Algorithm with Retraction and Vector Transport

assumptions_latex: For the natural filtration \(\mathcal F_k\), the sample \(\xi_k\) is independent of \(\mathcal F_k\).
The interchange \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{grad}_xF(x;\xi)]=\operatorname{grad}f(x)\) is valid at the iterates.
The stochastic gradients have finite conditional second moments, and the retraction is defined at every sampled step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recursion \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(-\alpha_kG_k)\), with \(G_k=\operatorname{grad}_xF(x_k;\xi_k)\), defines the online Riemannian stochastic-gradient sequence.

notation.meaning: Information generated before drawing the sample at iteration k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unbiased single-sample stochastic-gradient recursion expressed through a retraction
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-sample stochastic-gradient iteration for an expectation objective on a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\mathbb E_{\xi}[F(x;\xi)]\) on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), and let \(\mathcal F_k\) denote the information available before sampling at iteration \(k\). Given \(x_0\in\mathcal M\) and step sizes \(\alpha_k>0\), draw \(\xi_k\) independently of \(\mathcal F_k\), form the single-sample Riemannian gradient
\[G_k=\operatorname{grad}_xF(x_k;\xi_k)\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M,\]
and update
\[x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(-\alpha_kG_k).\]
When differentiation and expectation can be interchanged, \(\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\). The iteration stops after a prescribed sample budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Online Riemannian stochastic gradient draws one fresh sample, computes its tangent-space gradient, and retracts a negative stochastic-gradient step. Under the interchange and independence assumptions, the sampled gradient is conditionally unbiased.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Riemannian Stochastic Gradient
Minibatch Riemannian Stochastic Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent minibatch averaging of tangent stochastic gradients before a retracted update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\mathbb E_{\xi}[F(x;\xi)]\). At iteration \(k\), draw conditionally independent samples \(\xi_{k,1},\ldots,\xi_{k,b_k}\), form
\[\bar G_k=\frac1{b_k}\sum_{i=1}^{b_k}\operatorname{grad}_xF(x_k;\xi_{k,i})\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M,\]
and update \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(-\alpha_k\bar G_k)\). If each sample gradient is unbiased with conditional variance at most \(\nu^2\), then \(\mathbb E[\bar G_k\mid x_k]=\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\) and \(\mathbb E[\lVert\bar G_k-\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert^2\mid x_k]\le\nu^2/b_k\). Stop after a prescribed sample or iteration budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minibatch Riemannian SGD averages independent tangent sample gradients, reducing conditional variance by the batch size before retracting the step.
assumptions_latex: Sample gradients are conditionally independent and unbiased at \(x_k\).
Each sample gradient has conditional variance at most \(\nu^2\).
\(R\) is defined at the averaged step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minibatch estimator is unbiased and has conditional variance at most \(\nu^2/b_k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: variance reduction for an average of conditionally independent unbiased tangent vectors

children.title: Intrinsic Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaging families defined through intrinsic manifold geometry.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is a complete Riemannian manifold with distance \(d\).
The iterates \(x_0,\ldots,x_T\) lie in a geodesically convex set on which the stated minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar x_T\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathcal M}\sum_{k=0}^{T}w_k d(y,x_k)^2.\] If the displayed minimizer is unique, intrinsic averaging defines a single output; otherwise an explicit minimizer-selection rule is required.

notation.meaning: Riemannian distance induced by the metric
intrinsic weighted average of the iterates

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted Fréchet means are the standard intrinsic replacement for Euclidean iterate averages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a weighted Fréchet mean and permits nonuniqueness outside a suitable convex neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given iterates \(x_0,\ldots,x_T\in\mathcal M\) and nonnegative weights \(w_0,ldots,w_T\) with positive total weight, an intrinsic iterate average is any weighted Fréchet mean
\[\bar x_T\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathcal M}\sum_{k=0}^{T}w_k d(y,x_k)^2.\]
Normalization of the weights does not change the minimizer. When the squared-distance objective is strictly geodesically convex on a set containing the iterates, \(\bar x_T\) is unique. Without that condition, the average is set-valued and an output policy must specify how one minimizer is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An intrinsic average minimizes the weighted sum of squared Riemannian distances to the iterates; it is a unique output only when that minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Iterate Averaging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation or inspectable locator supports the manifold-specific Fréchet-mean claims. In statement_latex, `w_0,ldots,w_T` must be `w_0,\ldots,w_T`. Also, strict geodesic convexity merely on a set containing the iterates does not establish uniqueness for the displayed minimization over all of \(\mathcal M\); the optimization domain and uniqueness hypothesis must agree. The definition content kind otherwise fits this leaf.

children.title: Retraction-Based Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaging families formed through tangent representations plus retractions.

assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a retraction on \(\mathcal M\), and each required local inverse \(R_x^{-1}\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar x_0=x_0,\qquad \bar x_k=R_{\bar x_{k-1}}\!\left(\frac{w_k}{W_k}R_{\bar x_{k-1}}^{-1}(x_k)\right),\quad k=1,\ldots,T.\]

notation.meaning: locally defined inverse retraction at the base point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: recursive retraction interpolation is a standard computable surrogate for intrinsic averaging
retraction choice and inverse-domain dependence require authoritative sourcing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an order-dependent recursive average using a chosen retraction and its local inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input iterates \(x_0,ldots,x_T\in\mathcal M\), positive weights \(w_0,ldots,w_T\), and a retraction \(R\). Set \(W_0=w_0\) and \(\bar x_0=x_0\). For \(k=1,ldots,T\), set \(W_k=W_{k-1}+w_k\), compute \(v_k=R_{\bar x_{k-1}}^{-1}(x_k)\), and update
\[\bar x_k=R_{\bar x_{k-1}}\!\left(\frac{w_k}{W_k}v_k\right).\]
The algorithm outputs \(\bar x_T\). It is well-defined only while every inverse-retraction evaluation exists; unlike a Fréchet mean, its value may depend on the order of the iterates and on \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The running average moves from the current average toward each new iterate through a chosen retraction, using the new iterate's fraction of cumulative weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Retraction-Based Iterate Averaging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this particular recursive inverse-retraction averaging rule or its order and retraction dependence. Every occurrence of `ldots` in mathematical lists must be `\ldots`. The algorithm content kind fits the output-policy leaf, but authoritative sourcing is needed to confirm that this construction is standard in the intended local sense.

children.title: Randomized Iterate Selection
children.top_down_role: Output rules selecting an iterate according to prescribed sampling weights.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\sim(p_0,ldots,p_T),\qquad x_{\mathrm{out}}=x_K,\qquad \mathbb E[\phi(x_{\mathrm{out}})]=\sum_{k=0}^{T}p_k\mathbb E[\phi(x_k)].\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: randomized output converts weighted iterate bounds into an expectation for one actual iterate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects an actual iterate and therefore requires no notion of averaging points on a manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose probabilities \(p_0,ldots,p_T\) before observing the independent output-selection draw. Sample an index \(K\) with \(\mathbb P(K=k)=p_k\) and return \(x_{\mathrm{out}}=x_K\). For every nonnegative measurable performance measure \(\phi:\mathcal M\to[0,\infty]\), conditioning on the generated iterates gives
\[\mathbb E[\phi(x_{\mathrm{out}})\mid x_0,ldots,x_T]=\sum_{k=0}^{T}p_k\phi(x_k).\]
Thus weights used in a convergence estimate can be normalized into selection probabilities without forming a manifold-valued average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample an iterate index from prescribed probabilities and return that iterate; its expected performance equals the corresponding weighted average of iterate performances.
knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Iterate Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source supports the stochastic output policy. Every mathematical occurrence of `ldots` must be `\ldots`. The conditional expectation identity additionally requires the output draw to have conditional probabilities \(\mathbb P(K=k\mid x_0,\ldots,x_T)=p_k\), or an equivalent conditional-independence assumption; choosing probabilities before the draw alone is insufficient if they may depend on the trajectory. The algorithm content kind is appropriate.

children.title: Best-Iterate Selection
children.top_down_role: Output rules based on observed stationarity or objective-quality surrogates.

assumptions_latex: A computable score \(s:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and deterministic tie-breaking rule are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[k_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le k\le T}s(x_k),\qquad x_{\mathrm{out}}=x_{k_*},\qquad s(x_{\mathrm{out}})=\min_{0\le k\le T}s(x_k).\]

notation.meaning: selection score, such as objective value or gradient norm

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite best-iterate selection is a direct output policy once a score is fixed
stochastic score evaluation and oracle-cost conventions require sourcing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best is relative to a declared score; noisy scores may require independent validation samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Evaluate a declared score \(s(x_k)\) for each candidate iterate \(x_k\), choose
\[k_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le k\le T}s(x_k),\]
resolve ties by the fixed rule, and output \(x_{\mathrm{out}}=x_{k_*}\). Then \(s(x_{\mathrm{out}})=\min_{0\le k\le T}s(x_k)\). Typical exact scores include \(s(x)=f(x)\) and \(s(x)=\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x)\rVert_x\). If only noisy estimates are available, the same guarantee applies to the estimated scores, not automatically to their unknown exact counterparts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return the candidate with the smallest declared score. With noisy score estimates, this certifies only estimated bestness unless additional validation is used.
knowledge_statements.title: Best-Iterate Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation or locator supports the output policy or the discussion of noisy-score validation. Every occurrence of `ldots` in the iterate list must be `\ldots`. Once a score and deterministic tie rule are fixed, the finite selection identity is correct, and algorithm is the appropriate content kind.

children.title: Averaging Ambiguity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Nonuniqueness, curvature, plus coordinate dependence affecting manifold averages.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M=S^1\) has its standard geodesic distance.
The two iterates are antipodal and have equal positive weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in S^1}\bigl(d(y,1)^2+d(y,-1)^2\bigr)=\{i,-i\}.\] Hence the intrinsic average is not uniquely determined.

notation.meaning: unit circle with its intrinsic metric

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: antipodal data on the circle provide a direct nonuniqueness calculation for Fréchet averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete cut-locus example showing that an unqualified manifold average need not be single-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Identify the unit circle with complex numbers of modulus one and use its standard geodesic distance. For the equally weighted iterates \(x_0=1\) and \(x_1=-1\), define
\[F(y)=d(y,1)^2+d(y,-1)^2.\]
The minimizer set is
\[\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in S^1}F(y)=\{i,-i\}.\]
Thus the phrase “average iterate” does not determine one point, even for two samples. Uniqueness needs an additional localization or convexity hypothesis, while extrinsic, retraction-based, and recursively ordered averages can select different outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two equally weighted antipodal points on the circle have two intrinsic means, so “the average iterate” is ambiguous without geometry and a selection convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Averaging Ambiguity Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The circle calculation is mathematically correct and the failure_boundary kind exactly fits the ambiguity leaf, but the record supplies neither a source reference nor an inspectable locator for this manifold-statistics phenomenon. A source is also needed for the broader comparison with extrinsic, retraction-based, and recursively ordered averages.

children.title: Geodesically Convex Stochastic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stochastic optimization behavior under geodesically convex objectives plus domains.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathcal M\) is geodesically convex and a minimizing geodesic between relevant points is selected.
The stochastic objective is \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\), with finite expectation on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(\gamma(t))\le (1-t)f(x)+t f(y),\qquad x,y\in C,quad t\in[0,1].\]

notation.meaning: sample loss for random sample xi
selected minimizing geodesic from x to y

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: geodesic convexity is ordinary convexity restricted to minimizing geodesics
samplewise versus expectation-only convexity distinction requires authoritative sourcing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines convexity of the expected objective; samplewise geodesic convexity is a sufficient stronger condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A stochastic optimization problem is in the geodesically convex regime on \(C\) when its expected objective \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\) satisfies, for every \(x,y\in C\), every selected minimizing geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to C\) from \(x\) to \(y\), and every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[f(\gamma(t))\le(1-t)f(x)+t f(y).\]
It is sufficient, but not necessary, that \(F(\cdot,xi)\) satisfy this inequality almost surely. The regime alone imposes no strong-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expected loss is convex along every relevant minimizing geodesic. Almost-sure convexity of each sample loss is sufficient but stronger.
knowledge_statements.title: Geodesically Convex Stochastic Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No authoritative source distinguishes expectation-level from samplewise geodesic convexity here. In conclusion_latex, `quad` must be `\quad`; in statement_latex, `F(\cdot,xi)` must be `F(\cdot,\xi)`. The phrase `every selected minimizing geodesic` is ambiguous: the definition must specify whether convexity is required along every minimizing geodesic in \(C\) or along a fixed geodesic selection. The condition content kind fits the regime leaf.

children.title: Nonconvex Stochastic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stochastic optimization behavior measured through stationarity or landscape structure.

assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,xi)]\) is differentiable on a Riemannian manifold.
The stochastic oracle is intended to approximate \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The target guarantee is stationarity, typically \(\mathbb E\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_{\mathrm{out}})\rVert^2\le\varepsilon\), rather than a global objective-gap guarantee.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: absent convexity, first-order stochastic analysis targets stationary points
precise oracle and smoothness hypotheses depend on the selected convergence theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the guarantee appropriate when no geodesic convexity assumption is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The nonconvex stochastic regime assumes neither geodesic convexity nor strong geodesic convexity of \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,xi)]\). Consequently, a small objective gap to a global minimizer is not generally implied by first-order information. For a differentiable unconstrained problem, the canonical first-order target is instead
\[\mathbb E\!\left[\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_{\mathrm{out}})\rVert_{x_{\mathrm{out}}}^{2}\right]\le\varepsilon,\]
or an almost-sure stationary-limit statement. Such a guarantee does not distinguish local minima from saddle points or local maxima without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without geodesic convexity, stochastic first-order methods generally target small Riemannian gradient rather than global optimality; stationarity alone does not exclude saddles.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Stochastic Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the claimed canonical target or its exact scope. Mathematical occurrences of `xi` must be `\xi`. The record should also distinguish a genuinely non-geodesically-convex objective from the broader unrestricted smooth class to which nonconvex analyses apply. The stationarity discussion is standard in spirit, and principle is a plausible content kind for this regime characterization.

children.title: Strongly Geodesically Convex Regimes
children.top_down_role: Enhanced stochastic guarantees under strong geodesic convexity.

assumptions_latex: The expected objective \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,xi)]\) is finite on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(\gamma(t))\le(1-t)f(x)+t f(y)-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)d(x,y)^2.\]

notation.meaning: selected minimizing geodesic from x to y

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the quadratic geodesic chord inequality is the standard strong-convexity predicate
convention for the modulus and admissible geodesics requires source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the quadratic chord-gap convention for strong geodesic convexity of the expected objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The stochastic problem is in a \(\mu\)-strongly geodesically convex regime on \(C\) if \(\mu>0\) and, for all \(x,y\in C\), every relevant minimizing geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to C\) from \(x\) to \(y\), and every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[f(\gamma(t))\le(1-t)f(x)+t f(y)-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)d(x,y)^2.\]
This condition implies geodesic convexity by dropping the nonpositive final term and, on a domain where a minimizer exists, implies that the minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong geodesic convexity adds a quadratic distance gap to geodesic convexity, implying ordinary geodesic convexity and uniqueness of an existing minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Geodesically Convex Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source confirms the modulus convention, admissible geodesics, or uniqueness consequence. Mathematical occurrences of `xi` must be `\xi`. The phrase `every relevant minimizing geodesic` must be replaced by an explicit quantifier or a defined geodesic-selection convention. Subject to that clarification, the quadratic chord inequality and condition content kind fit the leaf.

children.title: Convexity-Regime Transition
children.top_down_role: Changes in targets, rates, plus output selection across convexity classes.

assumptions_latex: The same expected objective \(f\) and geodesically convex domain \(C\) are used throughout.
Strong geodesic convexity uses the quadratic chord-gap convention with modulus \(\mu\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mu>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{strongly geodesically convex}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{geodesically convex}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{admissible as nonconvex}.\] The reverse implications fail in general.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the regimes form a strict hierarchy obtained by weakening convexity assumptions
rate consequences require separate theorem-specific oracle and regularity hypotheses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records logical nesting of regimes, not a universal convergence-rate theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed objective and domain, \(\mu\)-strong geodesic convexity with \(\mu>0\) implies geodesic convexity, while every geodesically convex problem belongs to the unrestricted class analyzed by nonconvex methods. Hence
\[\{\mu\text{-strongly geodesically convex}\}\subseteq\{\text{geodesically convex}\}\subseteq\{\text{unrestricted smooth}\}.\]
The inclusions are generally strict. Letting \(\mu\downarrow0\) removes the quadratic growth term but does not remove geodesic convexity; dropping the remaining chord inequality crosses into the nonconvex regime and changes the natural target from global objective gap to stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strongly geodesically convex problems form a subclass of geodesically convex problems, which form a subclass of unrestricted problems; weakening assumptions changes the natural guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity-Regime Transition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source supports the asserted strict hierarchy or transition interpretation. The conclusion phrase `admissible as nonconvex` is imprecise: a geodesically convex problem belongs to an unrestricted smooth problem class analyzed by nonconvex methods, but it does not thereby become nonconvex. The statement_latex expresses the intended inclusion more accurately. Property is the correct content kind for this transition leaf.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is lower bounded and \(L\)-smooth along the retraction steps used by the algorithm.
Given \(x_k\), the oracle satisfies \(\mathbb E[g_k\mid x_k]=\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\) and \(\mathbb E[\lVert g_k-\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert^2\mid x_k]\le\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathbb E\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_K)\rVert^2\le\frac{2(f(x_0)-f_*)}{\eta T}+L\eta\sigma^2.\]

notation.meaning: uniform random index in the first T iterates

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the bound follows the standard smooth stochastic-gradient descent inequality with a randomized iterate
exact retraction-smoothness convention and constants require a manifold-specific theorem source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A constant-step, unbiased-oracle bound for a uniformly selected pre-update iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Run \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(-\eta g_k)\) for \(k=0,ldots,T-1\), and choose \(K\) uniformly from \(\{0,ldots,T-1\}\), independently conditional on the trajectory. Under the stated retraction-smoothness and oracle assumptions,
\[\mathbb E\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_K)\rVert_{x_K}^{2}\le\frac{2(f(x_0)-f_*)}{\eta T}+L\eta\sigma^2.\]
Thus choosing \(\eta\) on the order of \(T^{-1/2}\) gives expected squared-gradient order \(T^{-1/2}\), and obtaining tolerance \(\varepsilon\) requires order \(\varepsilon^{-2}\) stochastic-gradient calls when the variance is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With unbiased bounded-variance gradients, constant-step Riemannian SGD yields a descent term plus a variance floor; a tuned step gives squared-gradient complexity of order epsilon^-2.
knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Stationarity Rate Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact manifold rate, constants, retraction-smoothness convention, and oracle complexity consequence have no supporting theorem citation. In statement_latex, both occurrences of `ldots` must be `\ldots`. Conditional unbiasedness and variance should be stated relative to the algorithmic filtration, not merely conditional on \(x_k\), unless \(x_k\) is proved sufficient. Complexity_bound is appropriate for the exact rate-family container, but the formula is unreliable without a manifold-specific source.

assumptions_latex: The iterates remain almost surely in a compact set where \(f\) is lower bounded and has Lipschitz Riemannian gradient.
The oracle is conditionally unbiased with uniformly bounded conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(x_k)\ \text{converges almost surely},\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert^2<\infty\ \text{almost surely},\qquad \liminf_{k\to\infty}\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert=0.\]

notation.meaning: Riemannian gradient of the expected objective

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Robbins-Monro steps and a supermartingale descent estimate yield weighted-gradient summability
manifold-specific theorem needed to confirm retraction and compactness hypotheses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A Robbins-Monro-type conclusion; it asserts stationary subsequences, not convergence to a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider retraction-based stochastic gradient iterates \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(-\eta_k g_k)\). Under the stated compactness, smoothness, unbiasedness, moment, and step-size assumptions, the objective values \(f(x_k)\) converge almost surely and
\[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert_{x_k}^{2}<\infty\quad\text{almost surely}.\]
Because \(\sum_k\eta_k=\infty\), it follows that
\[\liminf_{k\to\infty}\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert_{x_k}=0\quad\text{almost surely}.\]
Convergence of the entire iterate sequence or of the gradient norms requires additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness, unbiased bounded-moment noise, and Robbins-Monro steps, objective values converge and weighted squared gradients are summable, yielding stationary subsequences almost surely.
knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Sure Convergence Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No manifold-specific theorem citation supports simultaneous almost-sure objective convergence, weighted-gradient summability, and the liminf conclusion under exactly these hypotheses. The oracle assumptions need an explicit filtration, and the retraction/descent regularity needed by the supermartingale argument is not stated precisely. The theorem content kind fits the convergence-family leaf, but its hypotheses and conclusion require authoritative verification.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a geodesically convex subset of a Hadamard manifold, has diameter at most \(D\), and sectional curvature is bounded below by \(\kappa\le0\).
The objective is geodesically convex and the unbiased stochastic subgradient has conditional second moment at most \(G^2\).
The algorithm uses constant step \(\eta=D/(G\sqrt{\zeta T})\) and an intrinsic averaged output.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathbb E[f(\bar x_T)-f(x_*)]\le\frac{DG\sqrt{\zeta}}{\sqrt T},\qquad T\ge\frac{\zeta D^2G^2}{\varepsilon^2}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb E[f(\bar x_T)-f(x_*)]\le\varepsilon.\]

notation.meaning: curvature factor, with value one when kappa is zero
diameter bound for the feasible domain
uniform root-second-moment bound for stochastic subgradients

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: geodesically convex stochastic subgradient bounds scale as inverse square root of oracle calls with a curvature factor
exact curvature factor, averaging construction, and constants need authoritative theorem verification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A representative Hadamard-manifold stochastic subgradient rate with explicit diameter and curvature dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\), and define \(\zeta=1\) when \(\kappa=0\) and \(\zeta=\sqrt{|\kappa|}D/\tanh(\sqrt{|\kappa|}D)\) otherwise. For projected Riemannian stochastic subgradient iterations with \(T\) oracle calls, constant step \(\eta=D/(G\sqrt{\zeta T})\), and a suitable intrinsic averaged output \(\bar x_T\), the representative bound is
\[\mathbb E[f(\bar x_T)-f(x_*)]\le\frac{DG\sqrt{\zeta}}{\sqrt T}.\]
Consequently, \(T\ge\zeta D^2G^2/\varepsilon^2\) suffices for expected objective gap at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For geodesically convex losses on a bounded Hadamard domain, stochastic subgradient complexity is order epsilon^-2, with constants depending on diameter, oracle moments, and curvature.
knowledge_statements.title: Geodesically Convex Sample-Complexity Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The precise curvature factor, constants, step size, projected iteration, and intrinsic averaging construction are unsupported by any cited theorem. `A suitable intrinsic averaged output` is insufficient to determine an algorithm or justify the displayed objective-gap inequality. Because these choices materially affect the bound, source uncertainty makes the mathematical claim unreliable. Complexity_bound is nevertheless the correct content kind for this leaf.

children.title: Curvature-Induced Degradation
children.top_down_role: Rate losses caused by comparison distortion, transport geometry, or restricted convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Induced Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies an additional stochastic-stationarity term caused by curvature or retraction distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable on a Riemannian manifold, and suppose a stochastic retraction method admits
\[\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb E\|\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\|^2\le \frac{A}{\eta T}+B\eta\sigma^2+C\kappa\eta^2\sigma^2.\]
Here \(A,B,C>0\), \(\eta>0\), \(\sigma^2\) bounds gradient noise, and \(\kappa\ge0\) measures curvature or retraction distortion. Curvature-induced degradation occurs when the last term is nonzero and asymptotically relevant; relative to the flat-model bound, it contributes the stationarity penalty \(C\kappa\eta^2\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature-induced degradation is the extra stationarity error attributable to curvature or retraction distortion beyond the corresponding flat stochastic-gradient bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and the retraction satisfy the smoothness conditions needed for the displayed descent bound.
The iterates remain in a region with distortion parameter \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_{\mathrm{curv}}(T,\eta)=C\kappa\eta^2\sigma^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the specific curvature/retraction penalty. Moreover, the term Cκ η²σ² is also classified by the coupled-regime candidate as a geometry–noise cross term, so its placement as purely curvature-induced degradation requires an authoritative source and clarified taxonomy rationale.

children.title: Noise-Induced Degradation
children.top_down_role: Rate floors plus variability caused by stochastic-gradient noise.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Induced Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the residual stationarity floor produced by persistent stochastic-gradient variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g_t\in T_{x_t}\mathcal M\) satisfy \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid x_t]=\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\) and \(\mathbb E[\|g_t-\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\|^2\mid x_t]\le\sigma^2\). If a constant-stepsize method satisfies
\[\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb E\|\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\|^2\le \frac{A}{\eta T}+B\eta\sigma^2,\]
then noise-induced degradation is the term \(B\eta\sigma^2\). For fixed \(\eta>0\) and \(\sigma^2>0\), this estimate guarantees convergence only to a stationarity neighborhood; eliminating the floor requires vanishing stepsizes, increasing batches, or variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent gradient variance creates a constant-stepsize stationarity floor proportional to the stepsize and variance.
assumptions_latex: The stochastic gradient is conditionally unbiased.
Its conditional variance is bounded by \(\sigma^2\).
The method satisfies the displayed averaged-stationarity estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup_{T\to\infty}T^{-1}\sum_{t<T}\mathbb E\|\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\|^2\le B\eta\sigma^2\).

notation.meaning: stochastic tangent gradient at the current iterate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conclusion follows from the assumed estimate, and the failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but no source supports that estimate or its Bησ² scaling for the intended Riemannian method family.

children.title: Bias-Induced Degradation
children.top_down_role: Systematic convergence errors caused by biased estimators or geometric approximations.

knowledge_statements.title: Bias-Induced Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes loss of exact stationarity when the stochastic tangent estimator has persistent conditional bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g_t\in T_{x_t}\mathcal M\) have conditional bias
\[b_t=\mathbb E[g_t\mid x_t]-\operatorname{grad}f(x_t),\qquad \|b_t\|\le b.\]
Suppose the convergence analysis yields
\[\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb E\|\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\|^2\le R_T+C\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb E\|b_t\|^2,\]
where \(R_T\to0\). Bias-induced degradation is the second term. If \(b>0\) does not vanish, the estimate leaves a residual no larger than \(Cb^2\), even when sampling variance is reduced to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent conditional bias leaves a squared-bias stationarity floor that variance reduction alone cannot remove.
assumptions_latex: The estimator bias \(b_t\) is well-defined in \(T_{x_t}\mathcal M\).
The unbiased portion of the method contributes a remainder \(R_T\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup_{T\to\infty}T^{-1}\sum_{t<T}\mathbb E\|\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\|^2\le Cb^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-bias formulation is coherent and fits a failure boundary, but the asserted squared-bias stationarity bound and constant C are method-dependent and uncited.

children.title: Coupled Degradation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where curvature amplifies noise or persistent estimator bias.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Degradation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers rate losses that cannot be separated into purely curvature, noise, and bias contributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a Riemannian stochastic method have a stationarity estimate
\[S_T\le R_T+D_{\mathrm{curv}}(\kappa,\eta)+D_{\mathrm{noise}}(\sigma,\eta)+D_{\mathrm{bias}}(b)+D_{\mathrm{cross}}(\kappa,\sigma,b,\eta),\]
where \(R_T\to0\). A coupled degradation regime occurs when \(D_{\mathrm{cross}}\not\equiv0\) and cannot be written as a sum of functions depending separately on \(\kappa\), \(\sigma\), and \(b\). For example, a term \(C\kappa\eta^2\sigma^2\) couples geometric distortion and sampling noise and disappears if either \(\kappa=0\) or \(\sigma=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled regime contains a nonseparable rate penalty involving two or more of geometry, noise, bias, and stepsize.
assumptions_latex: The displayed stationarity estimate holds with nonnegative degradation terms.
\(\kappa\), \(\sigma\), and \(b\) quantify geometry, noise, and bias, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{cross}}\not\equiv0\) identifies degradation not attributable to any single mechanism alone.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed nonseparability criterion is plausible, but neither this taxonomy nor the representative Cκ η²σ² term is sourced. A precise reference is needed to establish the intended coupled-degradation notion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian Stochastic Variance-Reduced Gradient Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epoch-based Riemannian SVRG using component gradients, a full-gradient reference, retraction, and vector transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a Riemannian manifold, \(R\) a retraction, \(\mathcal T\) a vector transport, and \(f\) an objective with component functions \(f_1,\ldots,f_N\) as specified by Problem 6.1. Given \(m_s\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) and \(\widetilde x^0\in M\), for each \(s\ge1\), compute \(\operatorname{grad}f(\widetilde x^{s-1})\) and set \(x_0^s=\widetilde x^{s-1}\). For \(t=1,\ldots,m_s\), sample \(i_t^s\) uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), choose \(\widetilde\eta_{t-1}^s\in T_{\widetilde x^{s-1}}M\) satisfying \(R_{\widetilde x^{s-1}}(\widetilde\eta_{t-1}^s)=x_{t-1}^s\), form \(\xi_t^s=\operatorname{grad}f_{i_t^s}(x_{t-1}^s)-\mathcal T_{\widetilde\eta_{t-1}^s}\!\left(\operatorname{grad}f_{i_t^s}(\widetilde x^{s-1})-\operatorname{grad}f(\widetilde x^{s-1})\right)\), compute \(\alpha_{t-1}^s\), and set \(x_t^s=R_{x_{t-1}^s}(-\alpha_{t-1}^s\xi_t^s)\). Finally set \(\widetilde x^s=x_{m_s}^s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each epoch, the method computes the full Riemannian gradient at a reference point. Each inner iteration samples one component uniformly, uses vector transport to form a variance-reduced tangent direction from current and reference gradients, and retracts a step along its negative. The final inner iterate becomes the next reference point.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ and }f_1,\ldots,f_N\text{ have the component structure specified by Problem 6.1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\widetilde x^s\}_{s\ge0}\subset M\text{ is generated by the stated Riemannian SVRG recursion.}

source_evidence.locator: Recent Developments in Riemannian Optimization / 6.1.2. Riemannian Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient Method / Algorithm 6.1

knowledge_statements.title: Snapshot-Based Variance Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riemannian finite-sum SVRG using a periodically refreshed full-gradient snapshot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), choose a snapshot \(\tilde x\), compute \(\tilde g=\operatorname{grad}f(\tilde x)\), and initialize \(x_0=\tilde x\). At inner iteration \(t\), sample \(i_t\) uniformly and set
\[v_t=\operatorname{grad}f_{i_t}(x_t)-\mathcal T_{\tilde x\to x_t}\operatorname{grad}f_{i_t}(\tilde x)+\mathcal T_{\tilde x\to x_t}\tilde g,\qquad x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t).\]
After a prescribed inner-loop length, select the next snapshot from the inner iterates, recompute its full gradient, and repeat. Output the final snapshot or an iterate sampled according to the convergence analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-gradient snapshot supplies a transported control variate that is periodically refreshed during stochastic inner iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a retraction and \(\mathcal T\) maps the required tangent vectors.
Snapshot epochs and stepsizes are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t)\) with periodically refreshed \((\tilde x,\tilde g)\).

notation.meaning: vector transport from \(T_y\mathcal M\) to \(T_x\mathcal M\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the snapshot-based leaf and the displayed estimator is a recognizable Riemannian SVRG form, but no cited algorithm specifies the transport, snapshot-selection rule, or output convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive-Estimator Variance Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riemannian SARAH/SPIDER-type recursion with periodic batch recalibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x_0\in\mathcal M\) and compute \(v_0\) from a full or large-batch gradient at \(x_0\). For \(t\ge1\), either recalibrate \(v_t\) from a fresh batch at \(x_t\), or sample a batch \(B_t\) and set
\[v_t=\frac1{|B_t|}\sum_{i\in B_t}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x_t)+\mathcal T_{x_{t-1}\to x_t}\left(v_{t-1}-\frac1{|B_t|}\sum_{i\in B_t}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x_{t-1})\right).\]
Then update \(x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t)\). Stop after the prescribed oracle budget and output the designated final or randomly selected iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transported gradient-difference recursion updates the estimator cheaply between periodic large-batch recalibrations.
assumptions_latex: The same sampled batch is used in both component-gradient sums.
\(R\) and \(\mathcal T\) are defined along every update.
Recalibration times, batch sizes, and stepsizes are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_t\) follows the transported recursive difference rule and drives \(x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t)\).

notation.meaning: vector transport between consecutive tangent spaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the recursive-estimator leaf, but the record blends SARAH/SPIDER-style variants without a source fixing the recursion, recalibration rule, batch model, and output convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Table-Based Variance Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riemannian SAGA-type estimator maintaining one stored component gradient per finite-sum term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), store pairs \((\alpha_i,y_i)\) with \(y_i=\operatorname{grad}f_i(\alpha_i)\). At iterate \(x_t\), sample \(i_t\) uniformly and form
\[v_t=\operatorname{grad}f_{i_t}(x_t)-\mathcal T_{\alpha_{i_t}\to x_t}y_{i_t}+\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\mathcal T_{\alpha_j\to x_t}y_j.\]
Set \(x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t)\), replace \((\alpha_{i_t},y_{i_t})\) by \((x_t,\operatorname{grad}f_{i_t}(x_t))\), and leave other entries unchanged. Stop after the prescribed iteration or oracle budget and output the designated iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transported gradient table supplies a SAGA-type control variate while one component entry is refreshed per iteration.
assumptions_latex: Each stored vector can be transported from its reference point to \(x_t\).
The component index is sampled uniformly.
The retraction update is defined for the chosen stepsize.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_t\) is the table-corrected estimator and exactly one table entry is refreshed at iteration \(t\).

notation.meaning: reference point and stored component gradient

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the table-based leaf, but the transported SAGA formula and one-entry refresh convention require a specific Riemannian SAGA source; none is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Transported Variance-Control Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Places control-variate terms from different base points in the current tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x,y\in\mathcal M\), let \(I\) be a sampled index, and let \(c_I(y)\in T_y\mathcal M\) have mean \(c(y)=\mathbb E_I[c_I(y)]\). A transported control-variate estimator at \(x\) has the form
\[v(x,y,I)=g_I(x)-\mathcal T_{y\to x}c_I(y)+\mathcal T_{y\to x}c(y)\in T_x\mathcal M.\]
If \(\mathcal T_{y\to x}\) is deterministic conditional on \((x,y)\) and linear, then
\[\mathbb E_I[v(x,y,I)]=\mathbb E_I[g_I(x)].\]
Thus transport makes the subtraction tangent-space consistent while preserving the estimator mean under these conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vector transport moves a control variate and its mean into the current tangent space, preserving unbiasedness when transport is fixed and linear.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T_{y\to x}\) is deterministic conditional on \((x,y)\) and linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_I[v(x,y,I)]=\mathbb E_I[g_I(x)]\) and \(v(x,y,I)\in T_x\mathcal M\).

notation.meaning: vector transport from the reference tangent space to the current one

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically coherent under fixed linear transport and matches the leaf, but no source supports it as the intended transported variance-control mechanism in this taxonomy.

children.title: Transport Bias
children.top_down_role: Systematic estimator error introduced by approximate or incompatible vector transport.

knowledge_statements.title: Transport Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies bias introduced when implemented transport differs from the transport required by the control variate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let an ideal estimator use a linear transport \(\mathcal P_{y\to x}\), while its implementation uses \(\mathcal T_{y\to x}\):
\[v_{\mathcal T}=g_I(x)-\mathcal T_{y\to x}c_I(y)+\mathcal P_{y\to x}c(y).\]
Conditional on \((x,y)\), with \(\mathbb E_I[c_I(y)]=c(y)\), its transport bias relative to \(\mathbb E_I[g_I(x)]\) is
\[b_{\mathrm{tr}}(x,y)=(\mathcal P_{y\to x}-\mathcal T_{y\to x})c(y).\]
Consequently \(\|b_{\mathrm{tr}}(x,y)\|\le\|\mathcal P_{y\to x}-\mathcal T_{y\to x}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|c(y)\|\); persistent transport mismatch can prevent an unbiased convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using mismatched transports for a sampled control variate and its mean creates bias controlled by the transport-operator error.
assumptions_latex: Both transports are linear maps from \(T_y\mathcal M\) to \(T_x\mathcal M\).
The mean term is transported by \(\mathcal P_{y\to x}\) while the sampled term uses \(\mathcal T_{y\to x}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_{\mathrm{tr}}=(\mathcal P_{y\to x}-\mathcal T_{y\to x})c(y)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebra is correct for the deliberately mismatched sampled-term and mean-term transports, but that convention is specialized and uncited. A source must establish that this is the intended transport-bias boundary rather than an artificial implementation mismatch.

children.title: Estimator Drift
children.top_down_role: Accumulating mismatch between recursive estimates plus current gradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Estimator Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes accumulation of recursive-estimator error between exact or large-batch recalibrations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_t\in T_{x_t}\mathcal M\) estimate \(\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\), and define \(e_t=v_t-\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\). Suppose a transported recursive update satisfies
\[\mathbb E[\|e_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\le(1+\rho_t)\|e_{t-1}\|^2+q_t.\]
Iterating this inequality gives
\[\mathbb E\|e_t\|^2\le\Bigl(\prod_{j=1}^t(1+\rho_j)\Bigr)\mathbb E\|e_0\|^2+\sum_{k=1}^t q_k\prod_{j=k+1}^t(1+\rho_j).\]
Estimator drift occurs when these accumulated amplification and innovation terms exceed the variance budget required by the convergence analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive estimator errors drift when multiplicative amplification and per-step innovations accumulate beyond the admissible variance budget.
assumptions_latex: The displayed conditional second-moment recursion holds.
All products and sums are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E\|e_t\|^2\) obeys the displayed accumulated-drift bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The accumulated scalar recursion follows from the assumed one-step inequality and the failure-boundary role fits, but no Riemannian estimator analysis is cited for that recursion or the stated variance-budget interpretation.

children.title: Snapshot Separation Effects
children.top_down_role: Bias or variance growth as reference points become geometrically distant.

knowledge_statements.title: Snapshot Separation Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates snapshot distance to the conditional variance of a transported control-variate estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[v=g_I(x)-\mathcal T_{y\to x}g_I(y)+\mathcal T_{y\to x}\operatorname{grad}f(y),\]
where \(I\) is sampled uniformly. If component gradients satisfy the transported mean-square Lipschitz condition
\[\mathbb E_I\|g_I(x)-\mathcal T_{y\to x}g_I(y)\|^2\le L_{\mathcal T}^2d(x,y)^2,\]
then
\[\mathbb E_I\|v-\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|^2\le L_{\mathcal T}^2d(x,y)^2.\]
Hence variance control deteriorates quadratically with snapshot separation under this condition, motivating bounded epoch lengths or snapshot refresh when \(d(x,y)\) becomes large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under transported mean-square smoothness, the control-variate variance grows at most quadratically with distance from the snapshot.
assumptions_latex: The transported mean-square Lipschitz inequality holds.
The estimator uses the exact full gradient at snapshot \(y\).
The sampled component gradient is unbiased at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_I\|v-\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|^2\le L_{\mathcal T}^2d(x,y)^2\).

notation.meaning: Riemannian distance from snapshot to current point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variance conclusion is plausible under the displayed transported mean-square condition and appropriate unbiasedness at both points, but the condition and its applicability to the intended estimator need a specific source.

children.title: Estimator Recalibration
children.top_down_role: Refresh, correction, plus synchronization regimes limiting persistent estimator error.

knowledge_statements.title: Estimator Recalibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resets a drifting variance-reduced estimator using an exact or fresh large-batch gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose recalibration times \(0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots\), batch sizes \(B_k\), and stepsizes \(\eta_t\). At time \(t=\tau_k\), draw a fresh batch \(S_k\) and set
\[v_t=\frac1{B_k}\sum_{i\in S_k}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x_t),\]
using the full index set when exact recalibration is required. For \(\tau_k<t<\tau_{k+1}\), update \(v_t\) by the prescribed transported recursive or control-variate rule. In every iteration set \(x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t)\). Stop at the prescribed budget and output the designated iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At scheduled times, replace the accumulated estimator by a fresh batch or full gradient, then restart the variance-reduced recursion.
assumptions_latex: Recalibration times and batch sizes are fixed or chosen by a stated stopping rule.
Fresh recalibration samples are conditionally independent of the past.
The intervening estimator update and retraction are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\tau_k}=B_k^{-1}\sum_{i\in S_k}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x_{\tau_k})\) resets accumulated estimator error.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits estimator recalibration, but the record combines exact and large-batch resets with unspecified intervening recursions and schedules. A cited algorithm is required to fix the intended variant.

assumptions_latex: The algorithm accesses individual summands only through the stated oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{IFO}}(\varepsilon)\) measures component-oracle calls needed for expected \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity.

notation.meaning: Riemannian gradient of component i at x

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\) on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\). An incremental first-order oracle queried at \((i,x)\) returns \((f_i(x),\operatorname{grad}f_i(x))\), possibly together with prescribed retraction or transport operations not charged as oracle calls. For a randomized algorithm producing \(X\), its incremental oracle complexity at tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) is the least number \(Q_{\mathrm{IFO}}(\varepsilon)\) of component queries sufficient to ensure \[\mathbb E\!\left[\|\operatorname{grad}F(X)\|^2\right]\leq \varepsilon^2.\] The expectation includes all algorithmic sampling and output randomization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incremental complexity counts component value-gradient queries required to return a point whose expected squared Riemannian gradient norm is at most the prescribed tolerance squared.

children.title: Full-Gradient Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Gradient Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts evaluations of the complete finite-sum Riemannian gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), a full-gradient oracle queried at \(x\in\mathcal M\) returns \(F(x)\) and \[\operatorname{grad}F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x).\] If an algorithm returns a random point \(X\), its full-gradient complexity \(Q_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)\) is the number of such complete-gradient evaluations required to guarantee \(\mathbb E[\|\operatorname{grad}F(X)\|^2]\leq\varepsilon^2\). Component evaluations used internally to assemble one complete gradient are not counted separately under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-gradient complexity counts complete finite-sum gradient evaluations needed to achieve expected Riemannian stationarity.
assumptions_latex: Every component gradient belongs to the common tangent space \(T_x\mathcal M\) at the query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One full-gradient call returns the average of all \(n\) component gradients at a common point.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Gradient Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts individual finite-sum Riemannian gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A component-gradient query selects \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(x\in\mathcal M\) and returns \(\operatorname{grad}f_i(x)\), optionally with \(f_i(x)\). For an algorithm returning \(X\), the component-gradient complexity \(Q_{\mathrm{comp}}(\varepsilon)\) is the total number of such queries required to ensure \[\mathbb E\!\left[\|\operatorname{grad}F(X)\|^2\right]\leq\varepsilon^2.\] Repeated queries, minibatch members, and all components used to form a complete gradient are counted individually.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component-gradient complexity counts every sampled component gradient, including each member of minibatches and full-gradient sweeps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minibatch of size \(b\) costs \(b\) component-gradient queries under this convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Cost Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact accounting conversion when full gradients are assembled componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an execution makes \(q_f\) full-gradient calls and \(q_c\) additional component-gradient calls for a finite sum with \(n\) components. If every full gradient is assembled by querying each component once at the same point, then its equivalent component-oracle cost is exactly \[q_{\mathrm{eq}}=nq_f+q_c.\] Consequently, any guarantee stated as \((Q_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon),Q_{\mathrm{comp}}^{\mathrm{extra}}(\varepsilon))\) implies the component-query bound \(Q_{\mathrm{IFO}}(\varepsilon)\leq nQ_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)+Q_{\mathrm{comp}}^{\mathrm{extra}}(\varepsilon)\). This conversion excludes parallel-time discounts and unequal component costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace each assembled full-gradient call by exactly n component calls, then add all other component calls.
assumptions_latex: A full gradient uses all \(n\) components exactly once.
All component queries have equal unit oracle cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_{\mathrm{eq}}=nq_f+q_c\).

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued accounting for algorithms using full and component gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an algorithm attaining \(\mathbb E[\|\operatorname{grad}F(X)\|^2]\leq\varepsilon^2\), its mixed-oracle complexity is the ordered pair \[\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)=\bigl(Q_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon),Q_{\mathrm{comp}}(\varepsilon)\bigr),\] where the second coordinate counts only component queries not already charged inside the first. Given nonnegative unit costs \(c_f\) and \(c_c\), the corresponding scalar resource cost is \[C_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)=c_fQ_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)+c_cQ_{\mathrm{comp}}(\varepsilon).\] Reporting the pair preserves information that a single scalar count loses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed complexity records full-gradient and additional component-gradient calls separately, with optional conversion to a weighted scalar cost.
assumptions_latex: The two oracle classes and the no-double-counting convention are fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{mix}}\) is vector-valued, while \(C_{\mathrm{mix}}\) depends on the chosen cost model.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory–Computation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting principle for finite-sum variance-reduction state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each stored tangent vector require \(d\) scalars. A table method retaining one transported or reference-point component gradient per summand uses \(\Theta(nd)\) scalar memory and can update only sampled entries. A refresh method retaining a reference full gradient and \(O(1)\) working tangent vectors uses \(\Theta(d)\) scalar memory but must periodically spend \(n\) component queries to rebuild that reference. Thus oracle complexity comparisons must report both query counts and stored state; neither memory profile alone implies a universally smaller query count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient tables spend linear-in-sample memory to reuse components; refresh schemes use dimension-scale memory but periodically pay for complete component sweeps.
assumptions_latex: Stored vectors have \(d\) scalar coordinates in a fixed representation.
Transport metadata and indices require lower-order storage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representative storage costs are \(\Theta(nd)\) for a component table and \(\Theta(d)\) for a refresh state.

notation.meaning: number of scalars per represented tangent vector
